Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to renew my request of yesterday to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) with reference to the salaries of employees in the Public Works Department.
Hon. WILLIAM PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works.) I have made inquiries, and Mr. OLIVER.
I find that the caretakers and the heating engineers in the public buildings at Hamilton have not received their pay. So the hon. gentleman's information was correct on that point.
When the one-eighth was granted, the minister said that would be sufficient to pay these men for April and May. Is there any special reason why this has been withheld?

I also made inquiry as to the reason, and I found that with respect to the caretakers and heating engineers the vote of last year was not sufficient to pay them for the entire year, and a portion of the one-eighth was used in paying wages for the month of March. Then with the remainder the accountant began in the eastern provinces and went as far west as he could. So the caretakers and heating engineers, not only in Hamilton but in other parts of Ontario and the west, have not yet been paid.
Has the minister taken the course of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and issued a circular to the public works employees throughout the country as to their working in anticipation? _

No, because I have great hope, and the accountant felt, that in the course of a few days a vote for these poor men, who must of course get their pay, as every hon. gentleman will admit, would be available. I did not think it was necessary to issue a circular just at present.
We are in very good humour now.
When may we expect that the Anglo-American treaties and the correspondence in connection with them, will be laid on the table? We were promised them before now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will inquire.
I understood the First Minister to say last week that they would be all ready in a few days.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that. I said I would lay them on the table as soon as they were printed. They were ordered to be printed at once, and they are in the hands of the printers now.

I would like to ask the government a question in regard to Bill (No. 157) which has been introduced by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith), an Act to amend the Railway Act. Is it the intention of the government to promote the

passage of that legislation during the present session ? The Bill is a very short one. it has only one paragraph, which is in the following terms :
iNo operator, train despatches or other employee who, hy the use of the telegraph, telephone, or other electrical device, despatches, reports, transmits, receives, or delivers orders or messages pertaining to or affecting train movements shall he required or permitted to he on duty for a longer period than eight hours in any twenty-four hour period, except in case of emergency, in which case any such employee may remain on duty for a period not exceeding twelve hours in a twenty-four hour period, and such excess duty shall not he permitted on more than two days in any seven.
In view of the frequency of accidents on our railways during the past few years, I would like to ask the government if it is their intention to have that legislation passed during the present session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is a public Bill, and must take its rank along with all other legislation of a similar nature. Whether 'this Bill and other public Bills should be treated exceptionally, is a matter as to which I could not give an opinion at this moment.

I would ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), whether or not there would be any objection to laying on the table a statement respecting the seed grain supplied in the west, setting forth the amount purchased by the government, the sum paid for it, the amount that has been sold to farmers under the terms of the arrangement either by this government or the provincial government and the selling price. I have forgotten the exact details of the arrangement, but the minister will understand what information should be given.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, the distribution is only just completed. The report is being prepared as quickly as possible to place before the House. It cannot be a complete statement, as the accounts will not be closed by that time. It will be of the nature of an interim report dealing with the subject of purchase and distribution. I hope to place it before the House within a short time but I cannot fix a date for bringing it down:

Would the proposed statement show what disposition the persons to whom the grain was distributed had made of it ? The object of the government in distributing the grain, of course, was to have it sown, and so a complete statement would show how many acres the party had sown. I have heard it said that considerable amounts of this grain had been sold by the parties receiving it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid the statement I have in process of preparation would not cover that point, but the point will be covered by a subsequent and complete statement. However, I think there is very little danger that any of the grain has been sold, as the price at which we have been compelled to supply it would not be attractive as a basis of transactions.
Would it cover the point how much of it had been paid for ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it will show that

absolutely.

I observe that a great many of the private Bills are going to the Senate in the first instance. I quite approve of that idea. There is no reason in the world why many of the private Bills -and, indeed, public Bills as well-could not be introduced in the Senate. But I would like to call the attention of the government to the circumstance that there is, if I remember the rules correctly, a great discrepancy in the fees required on the introduction of a private Bill in the Senate and those required on the introduction of a private Bill in this House. Besides that, the rules of this House make special provision for additional fees, where Bills are introduced after a certain time in the session. The object of that, as the right hon. leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will remember, is to have Bills brought forward, and the work on them done, in the early part of the session when the business of the House is not conjested. This particu-

Jar Bill, and other Bills as well, come to us pretty late in the session. I would suggest that, as the government have entire control of the framing of the rules of the Senate in this regard, it might be advisable to consult with the leader of the Senate with the view to having the rules of the two Houses made uniform on this point. It seems to me an unnecessary incongruity that a private Bill introduced in this House should pay a particular amount, while the same Bill if introduced in the Senate, would pay a smaller amount, or that there should be any such discrepancy in these fees.
Right Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER fPrime Minister). As my hon. friend (Mr. It. L. Borden) knows, the Senate is the master of its own rules. The rules prevailing there are of the Senate's own framing. Two years ago, when we amended the rules of this House, we provided new fees for private Bills and I think that, on the whole, the new rule is an improvement on the old. The attention of the Senate may not have been called to this matter. But my hon. friend knows that the Senate desires to do more of the work of the session. I shall deem it my duty to call the attention of the leader of the Senate to this matter.

the floor to-day we have been unable to understand him. He has been out in the country preaching provincial politics, and I would like to inquire why a minister occupying the high and honourable position which the minister occupies would descend so low as to
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That statement, I suppose, is withdrawn.

Yes, I withdrew it. I wonder why the minister cannot go into his own province and talk provincial politics without making use of the following language :
Starting on another tack, the Minister of Marine asked : 1 How is it that a man so ferocious for French Canadians and Catholics as Mr. Bourassa is, has allied hinvsef with an Orangeman of Ontario like Geo. Taylor to get Mr. Cousineau elected in Hull? '
And further :
Do you mean to say that an alliance between Mr. Bourassa and an Orangeman like Geo. Taylor is not provincial politics? asked the speaker.
That is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I admit that the charge made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is correct, that George Taylor does belong to the Orange institution. He is proud of the honour of belonging to it and he is also pleased to ally himself with the first to make use of this language in the province of Quebec ; Mr. Bourassa said :
He did not, however, want to raise religious questions, but wanted the two races to remain in peace under the British flag.
Any man who makes use of these sentiments can depend on George Taylor coming to his assistance, because the Orangemen of this country have a duty to perform and they have performed it from time immemorial up to the present. That is to grant free religious institutions all over this country, to maintain and uphold them. We have no objection to our French Canadians because they belong to the Roman Catholic Church and it is our duty to uphold them in their rights. I did go over to Hull to help Mr. Cousineau and I am very glad to say that the French Canadian people of Ottawa county elected Mr. Cousineau to support Mr. Bojirassa, to the great discomfort of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But, I do think it beneath the dignity of a minister of the Crown to go into his own province and among his own people and try to raise religious and race

cries. I am surprised at the hon. gentleman descending to such tactics in order to try to defeat a gentleman who, I am glad to know, is elected in the two constituencies he ran for and who will carry Quebec when he appeals again, as he did appeal yesterday to his friends there not to pay any attention to what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries might say and who made use of this language :
He did not, however, want to raise religious questions, but wanted the two races to remain in peace under the British flag.
Further :
Hon. Mr. Brodeur

Mr. Bourassa said :
-talking about George Taylor and Orangemen, had forgotten to say that he had voted ten or twelve times with iMr. Geo. Taylor for the abolition of the French language in the Northwest.
The minister did not tell them that. But, when he refers to ' an Orangeman like Geo. Taylor ' I would like to know what his meaning is ; I would like to know what he means by it ? Why did he not refer to the Orangemen sitting behind him ? For instance, why did he not talk about the hon. member for East Feterborough (Mr. Finlay) 1 Does he think that there are no Orangemen amongst the hon. gentlemen who are supporting the government ?
They were not worth mentioning.

No. But, the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, going down into his own province, trying to raise religious feeling and indulging in the language which I have quoted could have mentioned some hon. gentlemen who are supporters of the government at the same time that he picked out ' an Orangeman like Geo. Taylor.'
Are there any more of them there ?

There is quite a number, the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Finlay), the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Jackson), the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) and the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley).
The hon. member (Mr. Taylor) - is astray.

X think that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, while he occupies the position of a minister, ought to rise above race and religious cries in a local election instead of dragging in the names of men who are just as honest as himself and making references to Orangemen like so-and-so. The Orangemen occupy a high and honourable position in this country, the institution is just as high and honourable as any in this country either in the province of Ontario or of Quebec and we do not like the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to go on the platform and condemn and censure people as if they were not fit to be citizens of this country. They are citizens, they hold high places in this country and they will continue to do so.
What is my hon. friend reading from ?
I am reading from the Montreal ' Gazette.'
Oh.
The minister cannot deny it. I would like to ask the minister if he did not make use of this language.
Not in the way it is reported there.

A good deal worse probably in French. Does the government blame the opposition for obstructing when ministers go out and throw out such insults as this ? I ask the minister to say whether he said that Mr. Bourassa had formed an alliance with Orangemen like Geo. Taylor.
Answer.
Speak now.

If the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) does not deign to reply, I would like to say that such language does not come with very good grace from a minister of the Crown and especially from one who has so frequently referred to the fact that he desires to avoid race and religious cries in this country and that he always aimed at putting them-down and keeping them under. It is not a very good evidence of that desire and, if the hon. gentleman is correctly reported, I frankly confess that 1 do not think it is to his credit or to the credit of any minister of the Crown to make use of such language.

Before the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) goes on with his explanation I would like to read him a telegram which was sent to me, and if the minister could give us any information as to when the orders were given and what they were meant to signify I would be very glad. This telegram was sent from Moncton on June 5, 1908 :

Foster,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Following circular No. 190 has been posted in government offices here:
Division Superintendent's Office, June 3.
I have letter from general manager dated 2nd instant which reads as follows: ' I am instructed by department to advise you that the interior partial appropriation votes by parliament for works and staff under control of Department of Railways and Canals will shortly be exhausted, if not already so, and that no further appropriation has been obtained from parliament at the present date, and to instruct you to notify the general members of your staff of the position leaving it to them to decide whether they will continue to work on understanding that no salaries or wages will be paid them until further Supplies have been voted. Please he governed accordingly.'' Similar notices have been sent to employees individually. Is there any warrant for this circular ?
I think the minister owes it to the House to make a statement as to what he really intended to do by that letter. Did he intend to dismantle the Intercolonial Railway force or was this tantamount to a notice of a discontinuance of service ? If it was not meant for that what was the particular purpose the minister had in mind ?

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. F. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
The particular purpose the minister had in mind is I think quite clear on the face of the document itself. I do not see how any minister in charge of a department like mine could protect the department and himself under the conditions without doing something of that kind in view of what I will read now. On May 15 the Deputy Minister of the Department of Railways and Canals received the following from the Auditor General which I think will explain the whole situ-action :
Sir,-Let me call your attention to the fact that of a great portion of the estimates for 1909 only one-eighth has been voted by parliament. Please note that we have no authority to exceed this until further supplies have been granted. In view of discussions which have taken place in reference to the overdrawing of appropriations it would be advisable to notify all your officials charged with the expenditure of public money that they must not under any circumstances exceed the appropriation.
_ In view of that, the department did what it always does with contracts when the money has not been voted-it notified those interested that their salaries would be subject to supply being voted by the House. Suppose this had happened : Suppose parliament had dissolved and gone to the country it was well to have it understood that the money not having been voted the men could not be paid and until the money was obtained that they were working under that
understanding. It was simply that and nothing more.
Could not the hon. gentleman do as he did before and pay them when there was no appropriation by Governor General's warrant ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets that a Governor General's warrant can only issue when parliament is not in session.
I know that.
Parliament would not he in session under the supposition put by the Minister of Railways, namely, that there would be a dissolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was speaking of the present conditions under which the circular was issued.
Are not all the receipts of the Intercolonial at the disposal of the department ?
No.
When was a change made ?
The money goes to the Receiver General now.

By what Act of parliament was that done? When I was Postmaster General and when I was Minister of Railways the receipts were at the disposal of the departments if they choose to use them. Has the Minister of Railways any information from the Justice Department to the contrary ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has never been the case under the present administration, and I think my hon. friend is mistaken as to his own practice. I have not looked into the law, but I presume the practice has been in conformity with the law and the practice is that all the receipts from the public works of Canada go into the consolidated fund and can only be paid out of tile Dominion treasury when voted by parliament. I think my hon. friend is mistaken when he says it was otherwise in his day.

I am not mistaken at all. When I was Postmaster General and Minister of Railways I got an opinion from the Justice Department that all the receipts were at the disposition of the department of Railways and Canals and of the Post Office Department. Unless that has been changed there is no necessity at all for all this complaint about not paying the Intercolonial Railway employees and the Post Office employees. The Postmaster General has no doubt consulted the law officers of the Crown and he knows whether I am correct or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I still think my hon. friend is mistaken, but if there is a law which would allow any department to make use of the public money without the authority of parliament I think it is an unfortunate law. I am speaking of what has been the practice and I rather think it is in accordance with the law.

The suggestion made by the Minister of Railways was that there would be a dissolution of parliament and if that were so my bon. friend (Mr. Haggart) was correct in saying that a Governor General's warrant might issue. That is what tlie Minister of Railways put forward as an excuse for having issued his circular.
Not as an excuse.

I see fit to call it an excuse. The government might be driven to a dissolution of course, but I don't think they are likely to have any dissolution at the present time. The Minister of Railways has put forward a very poor excuse for the issuing of this circular. He gives the letter of the Auditor General as a reason, but the minister must have known the condition of tilings without the Auditor General pointing it out to him. Is the government driven to such a position that they must issue circulars to the employees of the government advising them to go on strike, because that is the effect of the circular. It seems like a political dodge and nothing else, and an attempt to relieve the government from the odium in which they stand before the people for their conduct of public affairs. No existing circumstance could have justified the minister in issuing such a circular. I thought it had been issued in some way without his knowledge, but now that he takes the responsibility for it I am amazed that he should have done such a thing. That circular was simply a bid to the men employed on the Intercolonial to ereat a political situation which is not in the interests of the country.

I do not want to be uncharitable but I incline to the opinion of my . lion, friend (Mr. Lennox) that it smacks very strongly of being a political move in order to make capitai against the opposition. If the minister had been perfectly frank he would have added to that circular that the reason the employees have not been paid is because of the minister's own neglect. The House met in November last and it was not until about twelve o'clock on Friday night, the 5th of June, that the minister deigned to ask the House for one dollar of this vote. If a gentleman who has charge of the Railway Department will sit in his seat for nearly seven months and not ask the House to grant him a vote of what is necesary in order to pay his employees. I think he is estopped from issuing a circular of that kind at this time. He
should have explained to them that by some strange mischance or lapse of memory or something of that kind he had actually forgotten that there was some $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 to be voted for them and that he had not during these six months asked the House for a dollar of that money. Does not the minister think he should have added that as a codicil ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways being known to be a truthful person could not have made that statement in the circular because it would not be the truth.
I am sorry to have again to point out that the Minister of Railways and Canals, through the Minister of finance, months ago approached hon. gentlemen opposite in the customary way and asked that the various public services of the country, including these particular persons in the Railway Department, might be provided for by a vote on account. We asked that a one-fourth vote might be taken, leaving three fourths to be the subject of debate in later days. Hon. gentlemen opposite, when approached in the usual way, did not concur in that suggestion; they accepted it only in a qualified way and agreed to assist us in obtaining a one-eighth vote. That one-eighth was duly obtained. When it was exhausted the Minister of Railways and Canals again, through the Minister of Finance, following the usual course, proposed a further vote on account, and we were informed we could not obtain the assistance of the opposition in passing that further vote through the House.
Mr. 'FOSTER. The Minister of Finance wishes to be given a reputation for extraordinary truthfulness.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ordinary.

For never allowing, even by inference, the least idea to get abroad that he is doing a thing not exactly as it ought to be, vide an example not long ago, where the Minister of Finance, when fairly cornered by the member for East Northumberland (Mr. Owen) as to the fact that he had already had voted to him some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 by this committee stated in effect that he could not be expected to come down for a Supply Bill for every $10 that was voted. That is an extraordinarily truthful way of representing the matter. A Minister of Finance who was cool and truthful and wanted to lay all the facts before the House, who was not unduly excited at the time of speaking, would say : I am very anxious to get the money so that these men can be paid. I have totalled up the items and find I have been voted some $7,000,000 or $8,000,000; here are these poor people waiting for their pay which is in arrears; I think as Minister of Finance I might take my dignity off my shoulders and ask a Supply Bill for $10,000,000 or $12,000,- _

000 and so get the money for these public servants. Did he do that? No. He is the minister who says :	You people in the
opposition have no rights except what we chose to give you. He is the minister who has grown very autocratical-three-fourths of the difficulty in this House is due to his autocratical or aristocratical disposition. Time was, I dare say, when he was a democrat, a democrat down to the hilt, like the right hon. gentleman beside him. Time was when he belonged to the common peo-' pie and stood for the virtues of the common people. To-day he has gone on in an interrupted course of events politically which he does . not seem to have ascribed to anything but his great ability and foresight, whereas, in reality, Providence and favouring gales have been behind him and certainly he would not be in the position he is if Providence and favouring gales had not assisted him. Now he has grown autocratical. He says to these employees: Starve if you like, I have $12,000,000 of your money and I will be hanged if I will ask to have it paid to you until the whole batch of estimates are put through. The minister must take the responsibility for his position in not asking a Supply Bill for nearly $12,000,000. He is not suffering, he draws his salary each month as it is statutory. but these men cannot do that and he holds them up. The minister would have done well if on having $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 voted he had asked for a Supply Bill. He would then have done well for the people who are .in need of the salaries which they have earned and which are due to them.
The minister has made the statement, not once but twice to-day, that the Minister of Railways and Canals has through him asked for a vote on two occasions. Of course the other ministers do not amount to much. The Minister of 'Customs is a small man and the Minister of Railways and Canals is a young man and they are modest and do not like to ask parliament for their votes and so the Minister of Finance says : Through me, the Finance Minister of this great and growing country, a vote is asked for. So when you tax the Minister of Railways and Canals with being too neglectful or having his memory not serve him well in this matter the Minister of Finance hopes to get him out of it by saying: Oh, that does not matter, I as Minister of Finance have asked for a vote on account on two occasions; on one occasion you gave us one-eighth and on the other you refused it. The Minister of Finance would be more truthful, according to his own statement of what he wants to get, if he had given I the attendant circumstances of that second asking. The Finance Minister knows and the Prime Minister knows that negotiations have beem going on, that there are questions in dispute between the opposition and the Mr. FOSTER.
government and that every request which has been made for Supplies in that way has been made on the basis of negotiations which at the time were going on, and that there was a reply which might have been made by the Prime Minister himself which would have lightened the situation but that reply was not given.
The Prime Minister is fond of saying that the ICing's government must go on. Yes, but it is an altogether different assumption that it must go on under the present flag. It is quite possible it might go on just as well under another party. The King's government must go on but that is not the statement that it must go on under the party which at the moment holds the reins of power. There are some things which are public measures and some things are not. This measure which is in dispute between the opposition and the government to-day is a measure which affects the status of members of this House. It is something in which every member is interested. In Great Britain these arrangements of the franchise of the country are matters of consultation and agreement between both sides of the House. You cannot find an instance in the British parliament of a minister undertaking to revise the basis of the franchise and putting it on this ground; I have a right to bring this in. I am going to put it through and you have no right to treat this in any other way than to discuss it and vote upon .it and see which side is the stronger of the two. They do not do things in that way in the British parliament, and never have done them in that way. This measure, therefore, fairly regarded, is not in, the same category as a public Bill, the Civil Service Bill, for instance, the Hudson Bay Railway Bill, or any other measure of that kind. This is a matter for negotiation and compromise, and in the negotiations that have gone on, the granting of Supplies has been a make-weight. The Minister of Finance should have stated that, and should have stated, if he had wanted to be frank about it, that the negotiations are still pending and that the Prime Minister is the man who has been in charge and has not concluded the matter.
Now, I have been frank in this matter, because there is no use in trying to make out before the country that there is not an issue between us, nor is there any use in trying to make out that the issue is different from what it is. Here you have the franchises of the Dominion; here you have a party in power which, during eighteen years of its history in opposition, maintained a certain view with regard to the franchise. They declared for a Franchise Bill on the lines of the provincial franchises. They canvassed the country on that; they asked votes on that; they got into power on it. So they had a mandate from the people on this subject. They came into power and they revised the law accord-

ing to the mandate of the people. Now, the Prime Minister has no mandate from the people to make ducks and drakes of the franchise arrangements of this country. Yet, without any mandate at all, they come before this parliament with a scheme which makes fish of one and flesh of another, which looks upon one province as being of a
Order.
What is the resolution before the chair?
The resolution is with reference to the granting of Supply. And making ducks and drakes of the basis of the franchise, treating one province in one way and another province in another way-
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is wandering away

-is not a proper handling of this great question. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance know that negotiations have been on the basis of this difference between ourselves with regard to this franchise measure. Now, is it not possible that this matter can be arranged and arranged quickly? Is it not possible that the Prime Minister himself can take a position which will get rid of this subject and remove the check that exists be-' tween the King's business and this parliament? That taken out of the road, there will be no difficulty, as my right hon. friend well knows. We should then have the disputed question put to one side and we could get on without the disputed question always continually obtruding itself and getting in front of the real business of the country.
How would it do for me to say a word or two just now. that my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) may know that I am in the House. I was away for a day or two
What were you doing?

I was talking about the obstructive tactics of the opposition. Now, to diverge for a moment before dealing with the question which I rose to discuss, I may say that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) might be a little more careful about the speeches he makes in this House. You have heard him, Mr. Chairman, scores and scores of times declare that the Liberals had adopted a platform in 1893, but, getting in power, had not carried out a single plank of it. He says now that we did carry out one at least -we amended the Franchise Bill.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Paterson) will allow me. I have heard members of the opposition make a statement on that point, but every one of them that I have heard has said that every plank of the Liberal platform had been sacrificed except one-that with reference to the Franchise Bill.

The hon. gentleman has repeated-and ' Hansard ' will show- that every principle laid down by us was violated-not one was carried out. Even the leader 'Of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has so far forgotten the facts as to state that.
When?
Many a time.
When? Tell me of one time.
I cannot recall them at the moment. I cannot recount exactly when the hon. gentleman spoke
I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) that he is entirely mistaken.

Then the hon. gentleman has sat in his place and heard his supporters make statements that were untrue and has not contradicted them. The hon. member does not deny that these statements have been made

I challenge the minister now-he wants to be very truthful -to put the statement before us :	When
that was made?

I am not playing this game of obstruction, understand. I cannot be drawn out in that way. I am within the judgment of the House whether that statement has or has not been repeated. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) alluded to the fact the other night that we had carried out this one plank and he has heard the
And now you want to override it.

I am not going into a discussion of the platform. It is a good platform. There is one plank that has not been carried out-the reform of the Senate. We had the plebiscite. The hon. gentlemau (Mr. Foster) will not deny that that is another plank that we have carried out.
I will not deny that the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) had a plebiscite.
The people
The people got no show in it.

Yes, the people voted in it. If hon. members cannot recall matters that have been of such great interest to the country it is a pity. Now, the hon.

member to whom I wisli particularly to refer is not present, but some of the others who spoke on the matter with which I wish to deal are here. They spoke of me as haying made a statement that was misleading and almost untrue. If I had done that, and my attention were called to it, I would at once take it back. But I cannot take it back and still tell the truth as I understand it. The member for East Northumberland (Mr. Owen) said :
The Hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) is reported to have said: 'In his department there were 1,800 men who could not get their pay because the Tory obstructionists would not vote supplies.'
And that he calls a misleading statement. But it is an actual fact, aud so I cannot take back my statement. Any one who contradicts that statement is making a misstatement absolutely. The men are not yet paid. I asked, when I came back, if they had been paid, and they said 1 No.'
And the bon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) said that he could send the cheques out if he got the vote put through.
If I said that, I said what was inaccurate.
And may be doing the same now.
It would be inaccurate to state that until these resolutions were embodied in a Supply Bill and passed the money could be used.

The hon. gentleman gave me the distinct impression, by explicit statement, that if the vote were put through he would pay his men, and the vote was put through with that understanding. It was on Friday, I think, and the hon. gentlemen pointed out that the vote then under discussion would pay the outside service, and said that if he got the otfier on Monday it would be in time enough, and the vote for the inside service was passed on Monday.
I could not get the pay for these men unless that vote passed in committee.
Does my hon. friend deny that he gave us to understand that if that vote passed, he could pay his men ?
What I gave you to understand was that it would facilitate the paying of the men.
Oh, oh.

Let me bring it a little closer home to the leader of the opposition. He knows that they wanted me to leave one item, he knows that when that item was passed they only let it go through the committee on the understanding that it was Mr. PATERSON.
to be debated on concurrence with the same latitude as that given in committee. Therefore so far as my getting the money was concerned, I was not advanced one step, lion, gentlemen opposite will not deny that. It is on ' Hansard.' Why did my hon. friend want the item to stand ? It was because, he said, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) wanted to discuss it. They found fault with me because I went to Brantford. But where was the hon. member for Brantford himself ? He was away when my estimates came up, and the whip of the other side said to me : Do not go on with your estimates because the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) is not here. I said I did not care, that I wanted to get the money. But we did not get my estimates through that night. We did not even get them voted through the committee although we sat until four o'clock in the morning. We were met by obstruction pure and simple-nothing else-obstruction undisguised and deliberate. We were told by the hon. gentleman then leading the House (Mr. Taylor) : Withdraw your Election Bill and your estimates will go through in two minutes. That was the statement made. The statement I made at Brantford therefore was absolutely correct. It accurately described the position to-day.
Is the hon. Minister of Customs going to resign ? He made a certain statement at Brantford and has had the verdict of his own county only yesterday.
But that was given four years ago.
There was a verdict yesterday too.

It was given four years ago but repeated with greater emphasis, so I am told, yesterday. I have no intention of resigning, at any rate until I have placed this matter clearly before the people as I did up there. The men are without pay because the Supply is not voted. Hon. gentlemen opposite ask, why not bring down the Supply Bill ? But concurrence must come first. When my items came to be concurred in, what would the leader of the opposition say ? He would say : We cannot concur because the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has something to say on the question, and it will have to stand. That is on ' Hansard.' To say that I made a misleading statement when I said that the government officials could not be paid because of the obstructive tactics of the opposition, is to make an utterly unfounded charge. Hon. gentlemen opposite did not wait until I was present to attack me. I went to Brantford, but not solely to take part in the provincial elections.

Of course not.

Mr. PAlERiSON. One lion, gentleman mentions the fact that I made no allusion to local politics whatever hut only to Dominion politics. I did take the opportunity of meeting the electors and putting before them the conduct of the opposition in this matter.
You got your verdict.

No, but you will get your verdict when you go before the people themselves. If there is anything in the minds of the people at present on which, when the government ask for a verdict, they will get a favourable verdict by an overwhelming majority, it is this question of obstruction. I can tell you that the rules of this House must be revised in such a, manner that while the amplest time will be given for the discussion of every question and the investigation of every subject, there must be a means devised whereby the bon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and the little clique of men around him will not be able to keep this House sitting indefinitely. That is the issue that will be pronounced upon, and the party which will favour a revision of the rules in order that something within the lines of decency may be maintained and the country's money saved, will be endorsed by the people, and the party which will be entrusted with the carrying out of that reform will be the party that has ever carried out all reforms.
Oh, oh.

All reforms that have ever been carried out in this country. Does any one suppose that these men could go to the country and ask the people to sustain them on an issue pledging themselves that if they came in they would pass an Act that would limit their own powers of oratory to something like decency ? It is hard on the civil servants and on members of parliament, but every day this obstruction continues, it strengthens the Liberal party. Therefore I can take some consolation out of it whilst being compelled to sit here and listen to the long windy, harangues made for the sole purpose of obstruction on the other side. My reputation for veracity I have fully established, and I will say no more.

One does not wonder that my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) should have come back in rather bad humour. Of course we must make some allowances for his spleen, and I trust sincerely that hon. gentlemen on' this side will take that into account and not lay too much emphasis upon the display we have had from him just now. The hon. gentleman entered into controversy- and that brings me to my feet-as to whether or not he gave the House to under-1 stand that if these items were put through
the committee, he would be able to pay his men. He refers to the fact that we asked him to hold over an item of $5,000. We did make that request, but then we let it go through because he pressed us to do so in order that he might have the whole item passed and therefore be able to pay his officers. Either he knew that when he was speaking just now, or his memory stands sadly in need of correction. Just look at what he said on May 29. It will be found on page 8738 of unrevised * Hansard ' :
Had you not better let me have this money now? The men need their pay.
Are you referring to the first item here?
It will be of no use to give us that, as it is only part of the item. The cheques can perhaps be issued if the items are passed, even before the Supply Bill.
I said ' perhaps.'
I think we will compromise by letting you have the first one, amounting to $1,815,000.

I will take that, of course, if I cannot get more; but I do not know whether the Auditor General will care to give a credit so that we can issue the cheques unless the whole item passes.
And the whole item did pass. It passed because of the representation of the minister that upon obtaining that item, he would be enabled to pay the salaries of his men. He went away the next day to the ridings of Brant and there he told the people that these men were without their pay because of the obstruction of the opposition.
Did you notice that I said ' perhaps ' ? You did not emphasize that. [DOT]
Do not let my hon. friend get any more uneasy than he is at present. He seems to be extremely uneasy.
Not at all.

I am sure the hon. the leader of the opposition does not want to be unfair. Look at the vote. That particular item referred to is only one of a vote of five items, and the whole vote could not be reported unless that particular item were passed.

My hon. friend need not be afraid, I shall read the whole record. The minister went on to say :
Besides, I want to go away next Tuesday, and it would oblige me if the item were passed.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend is very censorious of the hon. member for Brantford because he was away in his

constituency during the time of the local election. We did ask the usual courtesy that the minister would hold an item over until the hon. member for Brantford returned, and we were told by the Minister of Customs that he should be in his seat. But the Minister of Customs did not think it unbecoming his status here as minister to leave his position in this House and go to the ridings of North and South Brant for the purpose of taking part in the very same election. If it was wrong for my hon. friend from Brantford to go to his riding, how much more was it absolutely unworthy of the Minister of Customs to leave his public duties here and go to North and South Brant for the same purpose? The only difference between the two is that my hon. friend from Brantford has come back with victories in the two ridings to his credit, and the Minister of Customs has come back in a somewhat censorious and irritable frame of mind which has led him to make the exhibition he has just made. The hon. minister continued:
I am afraid that if we have two days discussion in order to get into Supply, I will have to go without it.
That is to say he placed his interference in this local election before the object of getting Supply to pay the officers of his department. He had to choose between the two, and he preferred to go to that riding to take part in a provincial election rather than remain here for the purpose of getting through with these items. Then he continued :
Will you give me the next item, which is for the salaries and travelling expenses of inspectors, as well as the salaries and expenses of the statistical branch here in Ottawa?
And I replied :
We will see about the others on Monday.
What did the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), say between ?

I am taking the discussion between the hon. gentleman and myself at present. The minister then said :
Will you let us get into Supply on Monday?
And I answered:
Did you ever know us to fail? A man who is not satisfied with a million and a half a day is very hard to please.
And my hon. friend then said:
It is really making a discrimination between the officers. Those of the outside ports will be able to get their money while those in Ottawa will not.
Could anything be more distinct and explicit? Yet this same hon. gentleman, witli these words still ringing through this chamber, went to the riding of Brant and said Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
that the opposition had prevented him from paying his officers, and he has endeavoured to impress us with his extreme regard for the truth in the face of these facts. I shall leave the record to the House so far as that is concerned. I then said:
They will get their salaries as quickly as the outside officers if you get the other item on Monday.
Showing the sense in which I most distinctly understood the hon. gentleman and the sense in which he wished to be understood. Yet he did not consider it beneath his dignity as a public man to make the misstatement he did make-I shall use no harsher word-in the riding of Brant. Let me refer to what took place on Monday

see page 9860 of the unrevised 'Hansard.' On the item 'expense of maintenance of revenue cruisers and preventive service, $40,000,' I said:
The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) desired to have some item reserved. Perhaps you will let the last item stand?

That would stop the whole item.
What was the advantage of passing the whole item? It was in order that the outside as well as the inside officers might be paid, as the hon. gentleman represented they would be paid if these items passed. The hon. Minister of Finance said:
The several items constitute one resolution, so that there would be nothing to report.
I then asked: Will you have any sup-plementaries? And the Minister of Customs replied
We may have, but I do not like to pledge myself that we shall have. Let the hon. member have the discussion on concurrence.
That was the hon. minister's own suggestion, with which he found fault just now. The hon. gentleman's memory does not seem to be very good. I then asked :
When does the minister expect to be back?
And the minister replied
On Monday next.
I then said
Suppose the hon. member for Brantford wishes to discuss this on concurrence, I suppose you will not have any objection to his speaking three or four times if it is necessary to answer you?
If it is necessary to explain himself.
As long as there will be some freedom of discussion.
I cannot promise about the rules of the House, but I do not think there will be any trouble about that. The fact is, he should be here.

The minister should not go away.

So the whole item went through on the tuti and distinct understanding that the money would be available, not only to pay the outside but the inside service as well.
When?
At once. Did not the hon. gentleman understand that?
No.

Need I read it again? Will the minister endeavour to grasp this:	He said
u is really making -a discrimination between, the officers. Those at the outside ports will be able to get their money while those in Ottawa will not.
Anything more distinct and explicit than that, I cannot imagine. AVhether the minister said something he did not intend saying, I do not know; but, his distinct words gave us to understand beyond doubt that if the two items, not only for the inside but the outside service, passed, he would be able to pay his men at once; and because of that representation, we let the item go through, so that there would be no discussion in that committee, even although the hon. member for Brantford had specially come to me and asked that some item should be reserved so that he should be able to discuss these estimates. He had also gone to the chief whip and left the same message with him. But notwithstanding that, I agreed to the hon minister's request in order that there might be no inconvenience, so far as his officers were concerned. We let the item go through because of the minister's representation that if they did those men would get their money at once.
The hon. gentleman has taken a position which is unworthy of him. His position is nothing but a perfect quibble, and he knows it.
Nonsense.

When I asked to have that item agreed to, it was because, as I said, that perhaps if it passed the committee, the Auditor General might give a line of credit for it, but I did not commit myself to that.
Why did you not say that in Brantford?

I said in Brantford the absolute truth, and I stick to it here. The hon. gentleman tries to cloud the issue and make out that I made a mis-statement, but he knows that if these men are without their pay it is due to the obstructive tactics of the opposition.
No, no.
Why then have the men not got their money?
You have not asked for it.

Yes, I have. If it were asked for to-day, what would be the statement we would be met with? We would be told that the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) was not in his place. And when the item came up for concurrence, the leader of the opposition would say that there was an understanding that it should not go through its final stage until the hon. member for Brantford was here.
How do you know if he would say that?
He would be bound to say it.
This whole discussion is out of order. I have allowed considerable latitude, but now have to insist on the House taking up Supply.
I agree that the obstructive tactics of the Minister of Customs should be suppressed.

Will you give concurrence on the customs estimates?
Mr. FOlSTER. Bring down your Supply Bill on your customs estimates and we will pass it right through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would like to have the railway estimates' concurred with it.
May be you had better not wait too long. After all this dignified discussion, has the Minister of Railways anything further to say in defence of the circular he issued?
My conduct in that connection needs no defence.
It is defenceless.

That there may be no misunderstanding about it, I will read these two letters. This letter was received by the department on May 15, from the Auditor General:
Sir,- 1 have to call your attention to the fact that of a great portion of the estimates for 1908-9 only one-eighth has been voted by parliament. Please note that we have no authority to exceed this until further Supply has been granted.
Now here is the important part:
In view of the discussions which have taken place in parliament in reference to overdrawing the appropriation, it would be advisable to notify all your officials charged with the expenditure of public money, that they must not under any circumstances exceed the appropriation.
That is dated May 15. Then on May 20 this letter was sent by the department to the various officers :

Sir,-I am directed to inform you that the attention of the department has been drawn by the Auditor General to the fact that of a great portion of the estimates of 1908-9, only one-eighth has been voted by parliament, and that until further Supplies have been granted, the expenditure must not under any circumstances exceed the appropriation. Be pleased to see that in dealing with the expenditures for work under your control this limitation is closely adhered to.
What was the date oil which you authorized that circular by Mr. Pottinger ?
The authorization of that circular would be the letter I have just read of May 20.

The minister's explanation does not help him out. I did not know that he has such timely notice, that he was told by the Auditor General on the 15th of May that his money had run out. and that he must take measures to replenish it; and it was not until June 5, twelve o'clock at night, that he mustered up courage to ask that this vote be taken into consideration. How does the minister excuse such negligence? Those on the Intercolonial that are doing their work and earning their pay, come up on pay day and find no money; although an intimation is given by the Auditor General on the 15th of May warning the minister that there are breakers ahead, and to look out. The minister lolls away from May 15 to June 5, that is twenty days, before he musters up courage to come down to the House and ask for money to pay his employees. In ail my parliamentary experience I do not know of such a case of lack of provision in a minister. May I ask another question:	Has the minister, been
paying out of advances made to him by the Auditor General, over and above what vote he has had?

Of course we had the
supplementary estimates.
I mean out of advances authorized by letter of credit or otherwise, by the Auditor General?
Nothing.

I would like to say to the Minister of Finance, in order to make this matter clear, that if the Minister of Customs really wants to pay his men, and he has not got through committee all that he has asked for, and has not up to this moment taken the additional step to make it available, if the Minister of Finance asks this House to make what the committee has granted available, they will do it in as quick a time as it is possible to put anything through this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That, so far as it goes, is very encouraging, and is a departure from the policy laid down by the hon. mem-Mr. GRAHAM.
ber for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), who said that we would not get one copper.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said so, too.
The Minister of Customs has made a statement that I ask him to retract or else make it good.
I think I can make it good.
Then I will accept your denial meanwhile.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I made no allusion to the hon. member for North Toronto in the matter, I am dealing with the official utterance conveyed to this House by that very responsible officer of the opposition, my esteemed friend from Leeds, who stated most positively and emphatically that it was the determination of the hon. gentleman opposite not to allow one dollar to pass until this devilish Bill-
I want to correct my hon. friend. I said I spoke for myself, only so far as I was concerned. Turn up ' Hansard,' and you will see it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is too modest. I am assuming that he spoke, at all events, with the authority of his long experience and great knowledge.
You are assuming what is incorrect.
He is only allowing twelve and a half cents on the dollar to go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then I will take the statement of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes) that, although the opposition are pretending that they are not obstructing Supply, all they have allowed, is twelve and a half cents on the dollar.'
That is all the government are worth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from North Toronto says they are willing to let the customs officers be paid. That is such a1 vast improvement upon the conduct of the opposition that I welcome it. Now why does he make a distinction between the customs officer, worthy as he may be, and an officer of the Intercolonial ? Is it fair to say : We are going to let the customs man get his money, but the poor man who labours on the Intercolonial must wait ? I appeal to my hon. friend, if be is so considerate of the other departments as he says he is now, and is willing to pay the customs employees, this vote for the Intercolonial, although it is a large and important vote, is one largely of a routine character ; - then why not pay the railway men as well as. the customs men ?

l.'r. PATERSON. In reference to the remark of the hon. member for North Toronto, I would ask him to look at page 9739 where he will find an interjection made by himself.

There is a very easy way for you to get them their salaries.
That is like what the hon. member for Leeds said : Withdraw your Bill, and you will get your money, and not otherwise. I am not, of course, a member of their caucus, but I know the papers stated that the hon. gentlemen opposite solemnly met together and determined that Supply should not go through until that Bill was withdrawn. The papers may have been wrong in that, I do not know.
The minister should not reveal what takes place in caucus.

I have verified my statement.
Mr. I!. L. BORDEN. I think if the Minister of Customs makes another record today such as that he has made in Brant, we will be willing to admit him to our caucus.

I am anxious to get this vote through, if possible. It is $9,035,000 for the Intercolonial, the Windsor branch and the branch in Prince Edward Island. If we are allowed to put this through, it is really being allowed to use the money that we have in the Receiver General's bauds. Any discussion on the management can be had on capital expenditure.

The Finance Minister asked why, if we were willing to let the item go through to pay the customs officers, we should not be equally ready to let this item go through to pay the expenditure incurred on the Intercolonial. There is a very great difference and a very much stronger reason why we should have it. In view of the disclosures which have been brought out by the Public Accounts Committee in regard to the jobbery, connected with the Intercolonial Railway in the last few years in the purchase of land and supplies and other things, we should have full information on each item before it is allowed to pass. With regard to the salaries of customs collectors we know what they are and we expect that they will be paid that money and that there will be no jobbery connected with them.
These items are really salaries. We will have a large appropriation for capital expenditure on which these matters can be discussed.
I was referring to the observation of the Minister of Finance.

As a matter of fact, as I understand, the receipts of the Inter-322
colonial Railway go to the credit of the Receiver General.
Yes.
And you are not able to utilize the moneys received for the purpose of meeting the expenses of the road ?
That is the position.
How many men are employed on the Intercolonial Railway ?
Will the minister tell us why he wants $1,400,000 more and also give us a statement as to what the receipts and expenditures are at the present time and whether they are falling off or increasing ?

The number of employees on the Intercolonial Railway is approximately 9,000

something under 9,000.
I would like to ask the minister if every one of the 9,000 employees of the Intercolonial Railway got the circulars which have been under consideration.
I have no idea. We sent the letter to the general manager.
The minister does not know how many circulars were issued ?
I do not.

Is it fair to suppose that each one got this circular ?
ilr. GRAHAM. Probably the heads of the departments got it.
You only want to get rid of the heads of the departments ?
We do not want to get rid of anybody.
My telegram said that ' similar notices were sent to employees individually ' and from other information we find that the circular was posted up in public places as well.

I cannot imagine that they would get 9,000 copies of this notice printed and send them to all the employees. I think that must be a mistake. The custom, whenever any change of rule is made, is that the notice is posted up so that the employees can see it. In reply to my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) instead of this being in excess of last year's vote by $1,400,000 it is really the same amount we expended last year, because, in the Supplemental Estimates, we had to ask for $1,400,000. The receipts are falling off as the receipts of other railways are failing off.
To what extent ?
The receipts fell off as compared with last year, lip to the 31st May, by about $180,000-for two months.
Is the Intercolonial Railway reducing its staff under these circumstances the same as the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway ?

We have not been doing it to the same extent. In order to find out the position of the railway with regard to its employees, salaries and wages I have asked for a complete list of the employees, the salaries obtained and the date of employment. I might further add that several of the brotherhoods have already asked for increases in what they call the schedule . and these matters will have to come up for consideration a little later on.
Would the minister give us a statement of the receipts and expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1908 ?
I will give the statement to my hon. friend after lunch.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to an article which recently appeared in the ' Daily Times ' of Moncton in which it is alleged that there has been a great deterioration in the Intercolonial Railway service aDd I would like to hear what explanation the minister has to make in reference to the allegations contained in this article. The article appeared on the 11th May and is as follows :
Mechanical department of the Intercolonial Railway in a deplorable state.
If the numerous reports being circulated by the railway men are correct, the mechanical department of the Intercolonial Railway is in a deplorable condition. The locomotives and cars are said to be in the worst state of repair known in the history of the road.
For months the Maritime Express trains have almost always been late. This results, railway men declare, more from inefficient locomotives than from bad coal, as recently reported; and as proof of this within a couple of weeks a new batch of locomotives, recently arrived from Kingston, have been running these trains with the result that a marked improvement is noticeable in the time.
These new locomotives, we presume, are like all others purchased for some years, paid for out of capital account. Indeed, it is declared by railway men who know a good deal of the working of the mechanical department, that if it had'not been for the additions to the rolling stock supplied the past year at the expense of capital the road would have been completely tied up before this. The policy for the past year has been to skimp everything not chargeable to capital so that Mr. Butler or Mr. Graham may he able to show as large a surplus as possible for the benefit of the electorate in the coming elections. The earnings for February are said to have been Mr. HAGGART.
very disappointing to the deputy minister and every expedient imaginable was enforced to keep the expenses down to March 31, the end of the financial year. As a result the shops here, and in fact at all repair shops, have not had force enough employed to keep pace with the work. We are informed there are no less than thirty locomotives lying in the Moncton yard awaiting repairs, and probably as many more at River du Loup, Halifax and other repair points. The hulk of these locomotives are said to he of the modern class and fit to do good work if they were only given the necessary repairs. Here in round figures is three-quarters of a million dollars worth of locomotives lying idle for want of repairs, and the minister reporting to parliament that the great development of traffic over the road necessitates the purchase of more locomotives and cars to provide for this increased traffic.
From the information we have there has been for some time sufficient locomotives and cars on the Intercolonial to meet all the requirements 'of legitimate traffic, if such locomotives and cars were kept in an efficient state of repair. According to the last report of the Minister of Railways, 23 locomotives were purchased between July, 1906, and March 31, 1907, and since that about as many more have, we understand, been acquired on the same account and more expected to be provided for in the pending estimates.
What we have said in regard to locomotives applies with equal force to the oars. Hundreds, if not thousands, of comparatively good cars are lying in sidings along the road awaiting repairs. Some of them have been idle for years and exposed to the weather are deteriorating very rapidly, and more are being purchased every year out of capital to keep the traffic moving. If only a royal commission of independent experts could he had to deal with the mechanical department of the railway, in onr opinion a state of affairs would he revealed that would shock the country. A scandal involving the loss of $50,000 or $100,000 to the taxpayers is the subject of comment all over the country. In this case there is a public investment of from twelve to fifteen millions in rolling stock. If a large percentage of this stock is allowed through mismanagement and wire-pulling to lie idle and deteriorate, is it not practically as had for the taxpayer as grafting on a large scale?
Only yesterday in Montreal I was informed by a very prominent citizen of New Brunswick that there were numerous complaints of deterioration on the Intercolonial railway, both as regards the operation of the trains and the road b^d. It was stated that ballasting was neglected, that in many places where ties were absolutely necessary they were not put in notwithstanding that last year the department bought .$100,000 worth of ties. It is also stated that several accidents which have recently occurred on the line resulted from deterioration of the road bed. Only a few days ago it was reported in the press that a train had two runs off between Montreal and Moncton. I would like to know what the Minister of Railways and Canals lias to say in reference to the allegations which are contained in

this paper which is published at the headquarters of the railway in Moncton and contains information which no doubt could he verified by the newspaper writer on the ground.
I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman when he .says these statements can he verified.
I said they are in a position to verify them because they are on the ground.

That is a reason why they should not make such statements because they are in a position to know better. That article complains we have not a sufficient staff and the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) suggested we should decrease the staff. Owing to the great increase of traffic all railways on this continent are endeavouring to reduce their expenses and the number of men employed, and some of them have shut up their shops for a considerable time. This article says we have not a sufficient number of men employed.

I did not so read the article. The article complains that repairs to rolling stock were being neglected, that new cars and locomotives were being bought on capital account while the railway lias locomotives which could do the work if they were put in proper repair, and, that this has not been done because it is the policy of the railway to scimp everything except what was chargeable to capital account so that a surplus might appear on working expenses.

Let me point out the absolute fallacy of the statement that last year every effort was made not to spend much money out of revenue but to take it out of capital so that at the end of the year we could show a surplus. Now here are the figures:	During the 9 months of 1907 we
expended on locomotives and repairs to same, $476,210.12; and during the year ending 1908 we expended on locomotives and repairs to same, $476,210.12; and during the year ending 1908 we expended $783,200.72 on locomotives out of the revenue, which is the largest amount that was ever expended out of revenue for this purpose. This shows that that part of the statement in the newspaper is not correct.
Does that sum you have mentioned not include the purchase of loco-mitives?
On repairs to locomotives we spent more money during the year just closed than ever before has been spent out of revenue account.
How, much did you spend on repairs to locomotives?

$783,200. including the purchase of 4 new locomotives.
