Oh, that is a mistake.
How many locomotives did you repair for this immense sum?
There is some mistake somewhere there.

Let me conclude the
statement.
Surely you know how many locomotives you repaired.
I have not that information here.
That would purchase about 40 locomotives.	.

I will get the information as to that afterwards but the point is that all this money came out of revenue and we expended more out of revenue for this purpose than ever before. On cars and repairs to passenger cars in 1907 we spent $166,813.88 and in 1908 we expended $310,21415. Now I am speaking of revenue alone, and take the freight car department-[DOT] during the nine months of 1907 we spent $327,050.24, and during the year 1908 we spent $604,984.64. This shows we _ have taken more out of revenue for the maintenance of the road in these threejlepartments than ever before so far as I can find the figures. The statement is therefore not well-founded that we are skimping that department. The excess of revenue over expenditure for the year ending March 31, 1908 was $16,000.
What was the expenditure on capital account for the year ending March 31, 1908.

Immediately after luncheon hour the minister should give us a statement with regard to the fiscal year just ended for which we have not yet seen the figures. It would greatly advance the items before the House.

The difficulty is in furnishing all the data up to March 31, 1908, We have not yet received that information, it has not come from the manager. We have a few items from the accountant which I have given to the House, but the general manager has not made any report and we have not all the information up to the end of the year just closed. I can give the information for the previous year but not for the year closing March 31, 1908.
The minister might give what he has. That would, I suppose, include a statement of the receipts and expenditures and a statement of the expenditures on capital account.
We will give all the information possible.

I asked the minister a question regarding one James A. Stewart. Tile parties advising the minister I think know perfectly well the James A. Stewart to whom I refer. But the man described to me was a brakeman of whom I was not asking at all. The James A. Stewart of whom I was asking is a gentleman who goes around on the different trains, jumping on at little way stations, checking up the conductors. In vulgar parlance he is known as a railway pimp.

My hon. friend was wrong in supposing that we knew the man referred to. There is a James A. Stewart on the road and there is a James Stewart. He asked for information about James A Stewart and we gave it. Now we will try James.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.
Perhaps the hon. minister will be able now to give some details about Mr. James Stewart who is a spotter on the Intercolonial Railway.

Of course my hon. friend will take back that expression ' spotter.' Mr. Stewart is a very useful officer, such as they have on all railways. He is a travelling auditor who checks up any place, either on the train or at the stations, he thinks necessary. Like all inspectors or auditors he does not notify people when he is going to make his inspection. I think he has been a very useful officer.

My information is quite different. I think that the term ' spotter ' is the one usually applied, but if it be not a proper term, I shall call him travelling auditor. My information is that this man makes himself objectionable indeed, not only to conductors on the road, but very often to others. I do not think you will find on any railway in this country, or in connection with any other work, any better class of men than the conductors on the Intercolonial Railway. That is the univei'-sal opinion held of these men. Mr. Stewart is not only objectionable to them, but also to the travelling public. It is said, for instance, that he will go into a pullman car, when people are in bed, draw the curtains and rouse them up, which certainly he has no right to do and which is exceedingly objectionable and improper, particularly in the case of ladies. It does not seem to me that this gentleman is a desirable person for the occupation given him, and I trust that the minister will look into this matter and see if he cannot replace this man with another -if it be necessary to have such a man, and I do not think it is with the class employed on the Intercolonial Railway-who can do his business without making himself objectionable to the employees of the road or the travelling public.

I can certainly second the remarks of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fowler) with respect to the character and the class of men who are engaged as conductors on the Intercolonial Railway. It has been my privilege and pleasure to give this testimony on may occasions heretofore. We also have a very high class of men engaged as station agents in charge of the stations along the line. Those agents have to submit to a regular audit. It is not an audit which takes place by prior arrangement, but very suddenly and at times unexpectedly. Those men do not complain of this. Men who are properly discharging their duty in any capacity have no right to complain of any audit, and I am sure that the conductors, so far as I have knowledge of those gentlemen on the Intercolonial Railway-and I know pretty nearly all of them personally-do not complain of the audit. I have had occasion to call the attention of the minister and his deputy to the auditor who has been named. Rightly or wrongly complaints are made of the manner in whicli he performs his duties, and I think that an inquiry has been made. If these allegations be true, he is certainly not a fit person to continue in the government employ, and I apprehend that the department are inquiring into that matter, if they are not, it will be their duty to. make an inquiry. Some time ago I called the attention especially of the deputy minister to allegations that were being made, and being made by those who would probably be in a position to know whereof they speak.

My information is that if thei'e were certain allegations they have never been substantiated. However, there is no necessity to discuss the matter. It is not necessary that any officer of the Intercolonial Railway should inconvenience the travelling public in the performance of his duty, and we shall not allow that. I shall have inquiries made to see how this man is performing his duty.
If the assertion be true that he opens berths at night, he should not be retained twenty-five minutes.

I have no personal knowledge, but I have been informed that such in the case. I am informed by most credible authority that that has occurred more than once. I do not want to do any injustice to Mr. Stewart, and I am not speaking from personal knowledge, but I am informed that he is not always in a fit condition to attend to his duty. That is very serious. The ex-minister (Mr. Emmerson) has pointed out that he has also heard allegations against this man aDd has properly drawn attention to the delicate position he occupies. It is quite different from that of an auditor auditing the accounts of a railway station. This man goes on

trains and is supposed to act somewhat in the position of a spy, and I do not use that term with all the meaning attached to it. I do not intend it in that way entirely, but he is there to see that each conductor gives a proper return of the fares paid in to him. Before there is any necessity for that sort of thing there must be a certain amount of suspicion in the minds of those who employ the conductors and set this man as a check on them, and I do not think that the result has shown any defalcation on their part. I should judge from the testimony which the ex-minister (Mr. Emmerson) has given of the conductors, that there would not be very great necessity for that kind of thing, and that it is not likely anything would result derogatory to the men from the inspection by this travelling auditor, as he is called. But it does not seem, from the information at hand, that any effort has yet been made to find out whether these allegations are true, no investigation has been held. It seems to me that the matter has been brought to the attention of the department by a person who naturally would have some influence in the department and whose word ought to be accepted, I mean the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) the ex-Minister of Railways. The ex-minister having made a complaint to the department, and having severed his connection with the department over which he had been for some years the responsible head, his complaint should have received a little more attention than apparently it has received from the present responsible officers. I judge from what the minister has said that no investigation of any kind has taken place, although these complaints are being constantly made and have been made for the last year or more with regard to the conduct of this man. It is said that he is not always in a proper condition to perform his duties. I do not know if that is so, but if it is, surely it is a matter that deserves very careful consideration, because it is one affecting not only the conductor who is doing his work in an unobjectionable way, but it weakens the loyalty of those men towards the department. Then again you are interfering with the comfort of the travelling public, which is another matter for consideration. For these reasons I think the minister should have taken some better measures than he has to ascertain whether these complaints are well founded.

Will the minister be good enough to explain what the duties of this man are ? Is he authorized to go along with the passenger train as a detective upon the conduct of the conductors and of the passengers ? It is hardly the proper way to treat a lot of conductors, who are supposed to be honourable men, to engage a spotter of this kind to go along with them.

1 have to leave in a few minutes, and I would lilce to say a word. It is but fair to state that I only called the attention of the deputy minister to this matter within the last few weeks, as it only came to my notice about then. Previous to that I had heard no complaints, either from Moncton or elsewhere along the line. When I did call his attention to it he told me that an inquiry would be made at once, and I have since understood from him that he had taken steps to have the matter inquired into, and if the complaints were confirmed he would feel obliged to call this gentleman to account.

In answer to the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburtou (Mr. Sam. Hughes), it is the custom of all great railway lines to employ men of this class to accompany the trains. The Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk, as every person knows who is familiar with railway work, have these men. I admit their duties are delicate, and ought to be performed with a great deal of care so as to give no offence, or as little as possible. They can stop at the stations and take a check of the tickets sold, and see that everything is carried on right. They can travel on the trains and check the conductors' tickets and passengers.
Why should he intrude upon passengers ?
He should not intrude upon the passengers in the way the hon. gentleman complained of. If he has done that, it is quite wrong, it would not be defensible.	.

The minister has spoken about the likelihood of an application being made from the employees on the Intercolonial or some of them, for an increase in their rate of pay. I think the minister might give to parliament a list of the various classes of employees and the rate of pay which is attached to each, so that we may be able to form an idea as to whether the rates paid are sufficient. I presume the minister has a list of the rates of pay of the different classes of officials, and he might take parliament into his confidence and let us know what the rate is.

I can get a list of that kind, but if I were to start reading it to the House it would be very tedious. I can get a list prepared and present it on any item of capital expenditure we may discuss later.

I am not quite satisfied with the answer of the minister with regard to this man Stewart. I would like to know what steps have been taken to investigate these complaints that have been

already made to the department, and what steps the minister proposes to take. It is a matter of great importance, both to the men on that road, and the people who travel upon it.

I understand that some such complaint as this was made publicly against this man in a newspaper some time ago, and on his issuing a writ to sue the newspaper, it apologized. I believe the complaint was made against two officials, and the newspaper apologized. I understand some complaint was made against them for misconduct on a pullman car. The only reply I can give is that this complaint has been shown to be untrue. However, I will make inquiry. We cannot permit that kind of conduct on the train. I cannot think that the newspaper report is true. No official would go through a pullman car and look into the different berths.

He might look into a berth to see whether it was occupied by one or two people, in order to make his check correct, to see 'whether the return the conductor was making was correct. X think the minister ought to agree to hold an investigation. You investigate matters of a much more trivial nature than this. It need not be a costly investigation. You have your road superintendents there, and you might charge one of them with holding a court of inquiry. You could very easily investigate by letting the conductors know that, if there were complaints against Mr. Stewart, they should prefer them at such a time. Or, you might do it by giving public notice. Any passenger who wishes to complain of having been misused by this gentleman in the alleged discharge of his duty, would be glad to know that he could go before your investigator and give evidence with respect to the matter. I cannot think it possible that the railway management desires to have one of its employees perform his duties in an objectionable manner. There is no reason why there should not be a travelling auditor, no reason why the trains should not be checked up. I find no fault with that, but I find fault with the manner in which this man is alleged to have performed that very delicate duty. I think the minister -ought to tell us that he will hold such an investigation. If he will do so, I shall be quite satisfied-and that should be a consideration with him, I think.

It is not customary to advertise for complaints. We might do a large business in them if we took that means. If any person will make a specific complaint of wrong-doing by this officer, giving some idea of time, I will be happy to investigate it thoroughly.

The minister knows the difficulty there is in getting anv one to Mr. FOWLER.
make a specific complaint. People will put up with a great deal when they are travelling;-they will grumble about it and will avoid the road if they can find any other way to go; but when it comes to making a complaint and making a court matter of it, that is entirely different. The knowledge of this fact probably encourages this man to go in his improper course. And so with the conductors-they do not like to make a complaint, for fear there will be a black mark against them so far as the management is concerned. But this matter can be investigated by the proper officials.. It is not necessary to advertise for complaints ; but if it were known that such an investigation were to be held, I am sure such complaints would be entered. At the present time, no doubt, the travelling public think that this kind of treatment is part of the policy of the road. It injures the government, of course ; and, from that point of view, it would be better for me to have it go on; but I am speaking from the standpoint of the road and the public.

I notice that on May IS, the minister stated, in answer to my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid), that there were twenty-one locomotives belonging to the Intercolonial lying idle at Moncton awaiting repairs, two at Riviere du Loup and one at Campbellton. That would appear to bear out, to a considerable extent, the article I read before we rose at one o'clock, so far as locomotives are concerned. How many new locomotives were purchased by the Railway Department last year?
Does the hon. gentleman mean the last fiscal year-the year ending March 31st last?
Yes.
The report for that year has not been made-yet. We have been discussing the previous year. But I will get the information for the hon. gentleman if I can.

While the minister is looking that up, I would like to ask with regard to this amount of $783,000 which the minister snys he spent last year for repairing engines. He claims to have two hundred engines
There are 370 engines.
Well, $783,000 would represent between $5,000 and $6,000 each for 150 engines. Surely, there would not be repairs to more than 150 out of 370. There must be some mistake.
The hon. gentleman will see that the point we were discussing was how much we have spent out of revenue. I understand that there are four new locomotives in that amount.
The hon. gentleman sail it was for repairs.
Would not the four locomotives be charged to capital?
I would like to ask the minister if he has received any complaints of the condition of the road between Painsee Junction and Pointe du Chene?
We have had some complaint that the cars were not as good as they thought they ought to have for that section of the road.

Is the minister prepared to do anything to remedy this state of affairs? Perhaps he does not realize the importance of affording good accommodation on that part of the road. Passengers to and from Prince Edward Island pass over this portion of the road. It must be remembered that there is a large and growing tourist travel to Prince Edward Island. It is well known that the province is becoming, perhaps the best summer resort in Canada. It was first taken advantage of by the Americans, but now also by people from all parts of Canada. I have here a letter written by the late premier of the province in regard to this matter. This will show that I am not talking about this in any merely captious manner-the late Arthur Peters, premier of the province, thought it worth while to write to the Minister of Railways and Canals on this subject. The Steam Navigation Company, of Prince Edward Island, which is subsidized by this government, put on the route some of the best boats in Canada-some of the best boats in America indeed, affording accommodation second to no passenger boats in the Dominion. Had this government fulfilled their share of the contract as well as the Steam Navigation Company has fulfilled its share, there would be no complaint. But, on this part of the road between Painsee Junction and Pointe du Chene, there is very inferior accommodation. When a man has travelled by palace car from New York, Boston, Toronto, Ottawa or Montreal, he is not likely to be pleased if compelled to ride in a car in which all classes of people ride together. I will read what the late premier of Prince Edward Island said, and I hope the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham will take this matter more seriously.
Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa.
Sir,-The attention of the government of Prnce Edward Island has been called to the very unsatisfactory conditions of the Intercolonial Railway connection between Painsee
Junction and Pointe Du Chene, over which most of the passengers, tourists, &c., from New Brunswick, the United -States and western Canada have to travel when coming to this province. Prom information furnished to the government and which is known to be reliable, it appears that only one passenger car is provided between these two points to carry all classes of passengers and all kinds and conditions are huddled together-first class passengers (including ladies) being compelled -to travel with Indians, Italians and filthy persons of all kinds, the car itself being frequently in a dirty state and utterly unfit for a passenger paying a first class fare to enter and to travel by.
This was addressed to the Minister of Railways and Canals two years ago, and I think it presents a condition that the minister must take into account. This is a state of affairs which interferes with the travelling public in coming to tbe province in tbe summer time, and I liope it is not going to continue. I would like the minister to say wbat he proposes, now that the tourist traffic is beginning for the season, to do to remedy this grievance. This letter is addressed to him by tbe premier of the province.

What date?
Sir A MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) Dated the 3rd November, 1906. I would like tbe minister to say what be is going to do with regard to it.

I think, if my bon. friend had read all of that return, he would have discovered that steps have been taken and that we have given instructions to remedy, in so far as possible, tbe train service, because it is very important and it carries a large tourist trade to, perhaps, tbe most beautiful summer resorts in the Dominion of Canada. We appreciate very highly tbe line from Painsee Junction to Pointe du Chene and we have given instructions to remedy the conditions there, and we will see that they are carried out.

S1ARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) That is very unsatisfactory to me. The minister says that the return which I have in my hand contains what tlie government is going to do. It is not what tbe return shows it is going to do, but wbat is it going to do? How many cars is tbe minister going to place upon that line? Is he going to place a sleeper on that section of road? It is all very well for tbe government _ to put me off by saying that they are going to do something; let tbe minister tell us what they are going to do.
Sly hon. friend does not pretend that there has been nothing done for the improvement of that service. If he does be is wrong about that.
SIARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) What has been done?

Better ears have been put on, and that is really the gist of the trouble. I think it would be unwise to say that we would put a chair car or a sleeping ear on that branch of 14 miles. A first class car has been provided, and that is about all the accommodation that could be expected for that short distance.
MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) Is there a first class car and a second class car?
The Boston train runs through without any break to the port, and I am not sure how many cars are on the other train. There are some times four and some times five and, I think, always more than one.

MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) The Minister of Railways and Canals, some time ago, in this House, told us that they were providing some motor cars to run oil short lines, and I would like to know what progress has been made in regard to them?

We have purchased four of these cars. I may say there is a difference of opinion and that negotiations are now proceeding between the brotherhoods and the management as to the manning of these cars, &e. Personally, I have been on one of these cars and i am inclined to think they will be very practical, but up to the present time we have run them in but two places-St. John and Halifax. We hope in a short time to have them in service.
MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) When the question was discussed in this House the idea was that two of them would be operated on two short lines in my province.
I think that will be the ultimate destiny of two motor cars.
MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) when will the ultimate destiny come ?

When we can conclude certain negotiations now going on about the running of these cars. When we get those negotiations settled I think my hon. friend can rest assured that the proposition to put two motor cars on the island will be fullv considered.
MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) What did these motor cars cost?
About $17,000 each.
MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) What is the difference in the cost of operation as between a motor car and a train operated by steam power?
That is one of the questions under discussion. It ought to decrease the running expenses.

When the minister talks about trouble as to the manning of these Mr. MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.)
cars he seems to be very mysterious about it. What is the trouble? I think the House would like to know. The minister has had these cars for nearly two years. Sufficient experiments ought to have been made in two years' time to have enabled the government to come to a pretty satisfactory conclusion, to know how they are to be run and to judge as to whether they can be run as economically as cars operated by steam power. They have been running between St. John, Rothesay and Hampton. What has been the experience of them? I have seen them puffing around there and everybody staring at them, but nobody particularly riding on them and the general impression I got from train men was that they were a costly and not very useful luxury. We ought to have some conclusion that we could tie to.
I think that experience has shown that they will be more economical when we have them operating properly.
Why do you not have them operating properly?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Poster) used the word 'trouble.' I prefer not to call it that, but to call it a difference of opinion. We have been running a car at St. John and I think every person will agree that it has been a success there.
For how long a time did you run it?

I think for the whole of last summer. I know that they were running them when I was there last fall. The brotherhoods are inclined to think that they ought to be manned with a larger number of men than we think are necessary. That may look to be a small matter, but it is quite far-reaching. We want to start them on a proper basis, if possible. I think they will be a success eventually.
How does the number of men you employed correspond with the number of men employed on American roads that are using a similar car?

I am told that the American companies man their cars with one less man than our men think we ought to have on them. Of course, you can under- . stand that there is a little prejudice against an innovation of this kind, and it is not so easy to have it running as smoothly as it might.

Is there any additional expense entailed by reason of having an engine always ready to haul them into port? They seem to be like the old automobiles ; it was generally necessary to get a farmer with a yoke of oxen to haul them into town. The minister told my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Martin) that it

was the intention to unload two of them on to a branch road on Prince Edward Island. There would be no serious objection by the people living along the Intercolonial Railway to having two of them or perhaps the whole four put on the island. You might use one of them between Painsec and Shediac.
They have petitioned for one there.
Better let them have it. To come from the ridiculous to the sublime ; how many official cars have you ?
Does my hon. friend mean in connection with the road altogether ?
Yes.
We will call them government official cars, there are six altogether.

By whom are they used ?
'Mr. GRAHAM. One by the general manager, one by the traffic manager, No. 109 by the Minister of Railways, No. 28 is used occasionally.
By whom ?
By the ministers and other people.
What do you mean by other people ?

Wait until I get through with the list-No. 139 is used by the deputy minister and by the Prime Minister occasionally when lie requires it. The Ottawa is used by Mr. Schreiber consulting engineer when he makes official trips.
Do you keep that car fully equipped with a porter and all that sort of thing just to be used by Mr. Schreiber when he makes an official trip which is not very often ?
That car is used by Mr. Schreiber and occasionally by ministers when they require it. It is not kept specially for Mr. Schreiber although he does use it when he goes on Ills trips.
Has the minister looked any further into the question of charging tolls for passengers across the Fredericton and St. Marys Railway bridge ? I brought the matter to his notice some time ago.
We did take that matter up at the request of my hon. friend, but they are pretty slow in giving us a reply and I will jog their memory again.

The former Minister of Railways said he would test the motor car service on two sections of the road in my province ; one,
the section between Lake Verde and Port Vernon and the other the section from Montague bridge to Cardigan. The present Minister of Railways has not carried out that promise. He is testing these cars somewhere in Nova Scotia and if they are a success we won't get them, but if they are not a success he will send them over to the island. If you had a motor car on the short spur between Port Vernon and Lake Verde you would save an hour in time. The minister apparently does not appreciate how slow his trains are on the island. From Murray Harbour to Charlottetown is 50 miles and it takes four or five hours to do that 50 miles. One of the reasons for the delay is this loop line. I hope the minister will devise some means to overcome that delay.
To return to the official car question-these six cars are exclusive of the Governor General's car and the Railway Commission car ?
Yes.
Are there porters attached to them all the time ?
Yes.

Supposing there is a tour of inspection by the Minister of Railways with spme of his officials, who pays the" cost of the up-keep of the car during the time it is running ? Who pays for the eatables and drinkables ? Of course water Is cheap and we will confine the question to the eatables, presuming that there would not be anything on board but water. Who pays for the supplies ?
The ordinary travelling expenses are paid by the department. The minister himself pays anything above that.
What do you mean by the ordinary travelling expenses ?
The ordinary expenses on the car. After the official work is done I pay my own board.

Suppose the minister was to start from Ottawa to make a trip over the Intercolonial Railway accompanied by some of his officials, does the government pay the expenses connected with the food supply on that car ?
The department would pay the expenses of the minister and any of' his staff when making an official visit, but if he had any guests with him the minister would pay their expenses himself.
The minister would pay the guests' expenses?
I should think he would? I know I would.
The minister then has had no experience of that kind as yet so he is speaking theoretically.

The minister has never taken any guests with him on one of these official trips except his own wife, outside of his staff, except from one station to another where perhaps some of the members might travel or perhaps I would ask persons with whom I was doing business to come from one station to another.
That would apply to the other officials too?
I do not know.

The minister ought to know whether the department in ail cases pays the expenses incurred, that is all the expenses in connection with the upkeep of the car during the time the tour lasts, all supplies, &c., for the use of the official car are paid.

The railway pays when the official is on official business, or any person is using the car on official business. Then the country pays and it ought to pay, but if it is being used on any other kind of business the users ought to pay it themselves and do, so far as I know. I have no intimation that they do not.

The minister or some of his officials ought to know. Suppose for instance the Minister of Agriculture should go on a junketing tour, would he pay the cost of the car?
Mi1. GRAHAM. He would absolutely pay the cost of the car, every cent of it.
I know the Minister of Agriculture would want to.
And does.

The minister stated that there would be a surplus of $16,000 this year. It will surprise the country to learn that after the immense capital expenditure they have simply been able to squeeze out a $16,000 surplus. I am not living on the Intercolonial Railway, in fact I have only been on it once in two years. The state ments I have heard in regard to the road are from people who travel it regularly, and if these statements are correct the article read by the member for York this morning was none too strong. It is not a question of $16,000 surplus or $160,000 surplus; it is a question of efficiency and safety'. If what I hear is correct there is neither efficiency nor safety to-day on the Intercolonial Railway. I have perhaps been in a position to hear more of it than usual during the last six months as my home has been closed and when I have been there I have been staying at the hotels and have come in contact with the travellers, the men who do the great business of this country. You can scarcely talk to a traveller who will not admit that he is afraid to travel on the Intercolonial Railway. I asked one young man about Mr. FOWLER.
three weeks ago and he shrugged his shoulder and said:	Off again, on again, yours
again Flannigan. He expressed his opinion of the road as he found it. I have found others who said they made it a rule, if at all possible, to return to Montreal and the west by the Canadian Pacific Railway. If these are facts it is time the country understood it. If the roadbed and equipment are in such shape that it is not safe to travel, the people should know it even if the government cannot force out more than a $16,000 surplus. We know it has been very difficult for the Intercolonial Railway in the'last few months to keep up to time. The trains have been behind time almost every day and it is stated the reason is that the roadbed and equipment are not fit to run. It is also stated that the engineers and drivers have direct orders not to run over thirty-five miles an hour. I have heard these things from more than one source, I cannot vouch for the truth of the statements but I am giving the minister an opportunity to deny these reports if they are not well-founded.

I have to say that the Intercolonial Railway will compare with any railway in the Dominion of Canada as to its accidents per mile. Its roadbed is equal to any other roadbed on the continent. I know as many commercial travellers possibly as any man in this House; I am very intimate with many of them for many reasons, and four out of five of the commercial men from this end of the country speak in the highest terms of the Intercolonial Railway.
The gentlemen with whom I talked were principally from points west of the maritime provinces.

They must be east by west. If there is one class who speak highly of the Intercolonial Railway, it is the commercial travellers. As to rolling stock I think the Grand Trunk Railway has an average of 13 per cent of its motive power lying to one side for repairs. Ten per cent of motive power is a small percentage to' be in for repairs. The Intercolonial Railway at the present time has between 8 per cent and 9 per cent of its motive power off duty for repairs. The management and the people are not afraid to compare the Intercolonial Railway with any other road. I know, of course, that there is a prejudice against a government-run road whatever party may be in power and the question of whether company management with larger rates and a different system of control is not the most satifactory is always a matter for debate, but at the present moment, so far as the rolling stock, roadbed and number of accidents are concerned, I am willing to have the Intercolonial Railway compared with any road on the continent.
Have orders been issued] not to run beyond thirty-five miles an hour?

It is a customary order on most well-run railways in this hard climate to restrict the rate of speed at the time of the year when the frost is coming from the ground.
'Mr. LOGAN. I do not know that any member on either side of the House who travels on the Intercolonial Railway entertains the same opinion of that road as the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Ganong).
I have not expressed any opinion of my own.

My hon. friend has given some opinions which he has heard, although he himself has only been upon the road once in two years. If my hon. friend, who is a fair man, were to travel on the Intercolonial Railway as we do who live on it, he would not entertain such an erroneous opinion with reference to the road, not only as to rolling stock but as to roadbed. The roadbed of the Intercolonial Railway should be the pride of the people of Canada. Anybody who travels over other railways will realize that the roadbed is a level and sound roadbed, that it is kept up in good condition, and that it is a smoother road to ride on than other railroads, in Eastern Canada at any rate. As far as the service is concerned-* the courtesy of the officers, the maintenance of the road and the general condition of the roads-it will compare favourably with any railway on the whole continent. I do not deny that there is a shortage of power, not for express trains, but for freight traffic, and there is some considerable necessity for increasing the rolling stock. As far as the express service of the road is concerned-and I can speak as one who uses the road very frequently- I would rather take the Intercolonial from Nova Scotia to Montreal than the Canadian Pacific Railway, even if it took two days to go by the Intercolonial to one day by the Canadian Pacific Railway. So superior is the one service over the other that if the people, in my part of the country at any rate, had to choose between the two, they would not hesitate to give the preference to the Intercolonial. If my hon. friend travelled on the road as much as I do, he would entertain an entirely different opinion and not believe all the stories he hears.

I am simply giving the minister an opportunity to contradict these stories and have his contradictions put in print. I have no grievance against the Intercolonial Railway. I have simply stated facts which I could prove if necessary. I have asked the minister if he can controvert them and he has not seen fit to do so. Has he given an order that the trains shall only run thirty-five miles an hour ?

My hon. friend needs a reply again. I have told him once before that orders are given on all roads, at certain times of the year, in this very severe climate, to restrict the speed of the trains.
If my hon. friend travels very much he will find that he frequently travels at a lesser speed than thirty-five miles ah hour rather than faster.
Possibly the order, like the letter which was read, was given by some official of the road.
Will the hon. minister state what amount was expended last year on repairs to the roadbed ?
On maintenance of way and structures there was expended $1,636,950. That would include buildings.
How much this year?
For the nine months of last year, $1,112,038, a little larger in proportion.
In making up your account do you take into consideration the depreciation of your rolling stock? What is the average life of a locomotive?
About twenty to twenty-five years.
And a passenger car?
Perhaps a little less.
In making up your account, by which you show a surplus of $18,000, do you take into consideration the depreciation of your rolling stock?

Railway accounts are not kept that way. We are supposed to spend a certain amount each year in keeping up our rolling stock. We make up in that way what we lose by depreciation. No railway company takes any cognizance of depreciation in the value of its rolling stock because that is offset by the expenditure on maintenance and repairs.
If the life of a locomotive is twenty-five years, that would be 4 per cent on the cost which you would have to expend.
This includes four new locomotives.

If you have 370 locomotives, and the life of each is twenty-five years, you would need to buy nine new ones in addition to the amount spent on repairs, to offset your yearly depreciation. Last year you only got four new ones and you have used up nine. That would mean five locomotives short, and if a locomotive is worth $12,000, that would be a shortage of $60 000. Where then is your surplus?

My hou. friend is altogether too intricate. If this $700,000 repairs

or an amount approximating, is spent yearly, a locomotive will last more than twenty five years. Some of these repairs practically amount to rebuilding the locomotive, and you cannot apply to such a locomotive the twenty-five years limitation. Three-fourths of our repaired locomotives are practically new.

The minister then misled me when he said that the life of a locomotive was twenty-five years. Surely he does not mean that a locomotive will last twenty-five years straight away without any repairs. What he must mean is that twenty-five years is the average life, when kept in repair. A farmer, who keeps his farm wagon in repair, would he able to run it for twenty-five years, but at the end of that term it is probably no good. If he did not keep it in repair, he could not run it that long. So it must be with a locomotive. Has the minister made a fair allowance for depreciation having regard to the fact that the life of a locomotive is twenty-five years, and that consequently he requires to have nine new locomotives every year?
The minister said it was a matter of bookkeeping. It certainly is. And this whole surplus is entirely a matter of bookkeeping. What is true of the locomotives is true of the passenger and freight car: and the only way by which you can reasonably figure out a surplus is by making an allowance, the same as every other road does, for depreciation of your rolling stock. But the minister buys locomotives and charges them up to capital. I venture to say that the amount charged to capital on the Intercolonial is at least three times what the rolling stock is worth. And that goes on accumulating, because no proper allowance has been made for depreciation of rolling stock in years past.
The minister has not yet stated the number of new locomotives purchased for the year ending March 31, 1908.

The hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) is perfectly correct in the explanation he has given of what ought to be charged to capital and what to revenue. There are on the Intercolonial, I understand, 370 locomotives. Now, the life of a locomotive is twenty years-that is the time allowed by railways generally. In other words, five per cent of the locomotives need to be replaced each year. In the easg of the Intercolonial, there ought to be eighteen new locomotives bought. But, in order to make a good showing, almost all the locomotives are charged to capital account. There are only four locomotives on the Intercolonial charged to revenue, where there ought to be eighteen. The life of a locomotive, the life of a rail, the life of a car-all these things are per-

fectly well known, and, unless you make the requisite charge to revenue for depreciation, you do not know really where you stand. As a result of the government's method of book-keeping, you have a surplus this year of some hundreds-[DOT]-
Yes, $16,000. And this is after the bright promises that were made by the minister's predecessor, and of the charge of $4,380,000 to capital account.
Does not the hon. member (Mr. Haggart) think we had better get rid of the road ?
Better manage it properly.
How did you manage it ?

I did manage it properly. I had no such charges to capital account as you see to-day. I would like to know the receipts and expenditures of the last two months. The minister tells us that there is a loss of $180,000 on receipts. How do these receipts and expenditures compare with those of the same two months last year ?

We have not the statement of expenditure for the last two months. As ex-minister the hon. gentleman knows that, in the regular routine, we do not get these figures so soon. I have a statement merely that the receipts have fallen off.
You have the figures for April and May ?
The receipts, but not the expenditure. That is, I gave an approximate statement of the receipts, but we have not the detailed statement.

Why, within five days after the end of the month, the minister ought to have the receipts and expenditures. And, more than that, he ought to have from his officials an estimate of the receipts and expenditure of the next month. The officials ought to keep the minister informed on that subject. The minister asks us for the same amount as last year. Surely, lie does not intend to keep up the same expenditure if the falling off in business is to be $800,000 ? He must reduce his estimate of expenditure. IVhat is the estimate of expenditure for the year coming ?

My hon. friend will see that it is impossible to make an estimate of the receipts from the present conditions. AVe hope they will improve, and are rather disappointed that there has been a falling off in the revenue for the last couple of months. As I have said, the difficulty of

this discussion is that we are dealing with more than one year. There is the year ending March 31, 1907, the report for which is before the House, then, there is the year ending 31st of March, 1908, the report of which is not before the House, and now my hon. friend wants me to discuss the current year. I cannot give him details which 1 have not myself.
But the minister is before the committee asking for $9,000,000 to carry on the Intercolonial for the current year.
And asking for the same amount as last year.

Yes. And he ought to have the receipts and expenditures for the last two months, and also an estimate of the present month. And be ought to have an estimate for the year for which he is asking this $9,000,000.

The only way by which we can judge the business of this year is by the business of last year. Either the hon. gentleman or I, or any body else, can guess at what the business will be, but that is the only way we have of getting at it.

And yet we had the delightful promises of the minister's predecessor concerning the year just closed. On the basis of the information he had, he estimated a constantly increasing revenue, and a surplus of $700,000, $800,000 or $1,000,000. But I suppose all this work of imagination is finished and is not to go on under the present practical management. Still, the minister ought to be able to give us an estimate whether the revenue is likely to continue as it is or to improve. If there is to be an improvement he ought to tell us about when it may be expected to be-, gin and how it is likely the road will stand at the end of the year.

In view of what has occurred in the minister's constituency, he must naturally feel depressed and not in a condition of mind to give the sort of statement the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Hag-gart) desires. If conditions had been different in Brockville and throughout Ontario, perhaps the minister would have told us that he would have a surplus of a million and a half next year. Now, I would like to ask the minister the number of first-class cars he has on the Intercolonial, the number of second-class cars and also freight cars, baggage cars, coal cars and flats.

This return is up to the 3.1st of March, 1907, the latest we have. Locomotives, 370 ; first-class sleepers, 40 ; second-class sleepers, 38; parlour cars, 9 ; dining cars, 8; first-class passenger, 137; second-class passenger, 97 ; postal and smoking cars, 36 ; express and baggage cars, 60; box cars, 5,596; refrigerator cars, 909; platform cars, 2,780 ; pulp wood cars, 50; oil tank cars, 25; hopper cars, 1,114; coal cars, 471; stock cars, 123; auxiliary and tool cars, 21; convertible dump cars, 130; vans, 119.
Now. will the minister give me the average life of each of these classes of cars ?

I could not give that information definitely. The average life, I imagine, taking all the cars together, would be 20 or 25 years. I am told there are some cars in the service that have lasted 40 years.
Estimating the average life of a passenger car at 25 years, you have 137 first-class cars, that would be about six cars a year. How many first-class passenger cars did you charge to maintenance?
While the deputy is getting the figures, I may say that we spent $310,214 out of revenue.
That was for repairs.

The deputy will get more definite information. On repairs to freight cars, $310,214. This plan has been adopted by the management and the department. Of course the question of capital and revenue is one that we might discuss for weeks and weeks. You may discuss it with any railway on this continent and you will find the same adverse opinion. When railways do a good business there is more to expend out of revenue. We are trying to arrive at a basis by which we would get rid of this yearly discussion as to what should be charged to capital and what to revenue account. A year ago last April we adopted the method of charging each month up to betterment the sum of $25,000; to maintenance and equipment each month, $3,000. We hope in time this will adjust itself so that we may not have the same kind of discussion as to capital and revenue.
Two locomotives-switching.

211 60,000-pound box cars were fitted with end doors for loading rails, making 579 cars in all fitted in the shops to the end of March.

9 box, 11 platform, 1 oil tank, 2 coal-20 tons.
Carried.

press and baggage ears, 60; what would be the average life of this car-20 years?

The minister will notice how fair I am in giving him the benefit of every doubt in these calculations.
The figures are fair but the argument is all wrong.
I don't think it is.
You could not .apply it to any railway in the world.

Oh, yes, you can, you will find an article in the last ' Harpers' Magazine ' which shows how this matter is regarded by other railways, and which will prove that it is the practice of other railways. There are 17 Gondola coal cars and 171 other coal cars at an average of about $500 each which would give you a basis of 24 cars to figure on, which would be worth $12,000, and that you take almost the whole surplus for the depreciation of coal cars alone.
