About $1,600 for a 50 ton car.

If an honest and business like account had been kept showing the profit, and the real depreciation on the rolling stock, a depreciation which should be met every year out of your revenue, instead of having a surplus of $16,000 you would have had a deficit of nearly $800,000. That is the real condition of affairs. In order to put that road at the end of 1907 in the condition it was at the end of 1906 in the matter of rolling stock; in order to make up for the depreciation of your rolling stock between the 31st March, 1906, and the 31st March, 1907, you should have expended absolutely out of revenue $800,000 more than you did, to say nothing of the new rolling stock which must be required on account ot the extension of new business and which might fairly enough be charged to capital. I repeat, and I emphasize it that you should have expended in the year 1907 about $800,000 more out of revenue than you did to keep your rolling stock in the same condition as it was in 1906, and in the calculation I have given you the benefit of the doubt in every case and have calculated most generously in favour of the management of the railway. Therefore the Intercolonial instead of having a surplus of $16,000 at the end of the year has a deficit of $792,000 and I challenge the Minister of Railways or any gentleman sitting behind him to controvert these figures. X say that what I have pointed out is the business experience of all railways. The result is that to-day we have charged up to capital account rolling stock to an amount more than double, I believe three times, the actual value of the rolling stock upon the Intercolonial Railway. That
is the condition of affairs and I do not see why the minister is not ready to meet it fairly, instead of saying my argument is not in accord with the facts in regard to other railways. Railways are run as business propositions and that is the only business way of looking at it.

Railways are run as
business propositions but not according to the proposition of my hon. friend. No railway makes up its accounts as he says. They may approximate it but he cannot find any" railway on the continent that does it year after year, magazine articles, notwithstanding. In a good year railways expend liberally out of revenue but when the year is not so good they expend more liberally out of capital. Sometimes they raise money by issuing bonds, &c. If the member inquires he will find that is true. As I said, we did start on the 1st of April last year laying aside $25,000 a month in order to equalize, as far as possible, the expenditure between revenue and capital. Let me point out what has been done. We have spent more than $25,000 a month out of revenue in 1907-1908.
If I am wrong why should you ?

The hon. member is
wrong because he is extreme.

Well you are doing
something along that line.
Not to that extent and no railway on the continent does.
If we did it at all we should pay all possible out of revenue.

In 1907-1908 we have purchased 166 60,000-pounds box cars at $990 each, $156,400 ; 130 hopper cars, $73,060 ; five refrigerator cars, $7,950 ; 100 flats, $87,000 ; 9 stock cars, $81,000 ; 8 conductors' vans $13,120 ; one dining car from the Pullman Company, $27,150 ; one sleeper, $19,500 ; two express cars, $14,000 ; two postal cars, $17,350 four locomotives, ten wheel standard passenger locomotives, and on these we have paid $23,600. Thus in 1907-1908 we have paid out of revenue for the things I have read $443,467.50.
That may be but was that enough ?
I think it was plenty.
The minister has admitted the whole case.
Not at all.
Yes, because you have admitted the principle.

You can carry a principle to an extreme. The hon. member

takes a certain set of figures and argues from tliem. I can argue him out of doors, I can turn any man in Canada into a bankrupt in fifteen minutes, if 1 am allowed to lay down my own figures.
I was practically allowing the minister to make the figures. I was only making the additions and multiplications.
My hon. friend cannot apply his argument to any railway as he seeks to apply it to the Intercolonial Railway.

I say that is the way every other railway is conducted as a matter of fact. Would the stock of any railway be worth anything on the market if it was necessary for the railway, in order to keep up the rolling stock, to borrow from capital?
The Grand Trunk last year paid for 455 box cars and 55 furniture cars out of capital account.
Because they were increasing their mileage.
Where has the Grand Trunk increased its mileage in order to get the cars ?
So far as that is concerned, I say that no railway could possibly buy that out of capital account and keep up its rolling stock.
They did it last year.
The thing is absurd on the face of it.
But they did it.
Does the Canadian Pacific Railway ?
You said any railway and I gave the Grand Trunk.

I started with the statement that it might be necessary to take money from capital account to build rolling stock if there was an increased traffic on the road which required additional rolling stock and that is what occurred with the Grand Trunk Railway. But I defy the minister to show where the Grand Trunk Railway paid from capital account to keep up the ordinary rolling stock.
Nor have we. We had an increase in traffic and we bought more rolling stock.

According to your report you did not require additional power last year. If you had shown that your traffic had increased and consequently it was necessary to get additional rolling stock over and above what the road was supplied with, you would have an answer, but you have not shown anything of the kind, because in 1907 you did not buy any additional cars. You did not buy a single passenger-car. You repaired some box and freights and that is all you did.
My hon. friend is wrong.
I am taking the report here.

I read from revenue and that is wlmt the report says. You take the other line of argument and say if the Grand Trunk wants new rolling stock or new business they can buy it from capital. That is what we did. We increased our rolling stock in 1906-1907 not out of revenue but out of capital as the Grand Trunk Railway did.

You bought 20 new locomotives charged to capital account, increased equipment. If that were necessary on account of increased traffic on the road it would be all right. I did not discuss that point, I was taking the stock you had and showing what you had done in the way of keeping it up from revenue.
That has nothing to do with the argument.

It has. I put exactly on the same plane as the 200 or 400 additional box cars that the Grand Trunk bought by reason of increased traffic, 20 locomotives, 3 locomotives for switching and 115 hopper-cars. On account of your increased traffic you bought these but what did you charge to revenue ? Nine box ears, 11 platform cars, one oil tank and 2 coal cars. The others were repairs, fitting flat cars with racks for pulpwood, &c. Where you had increased traffic and by reason of that required more rolling stock, you would have a right to charge that to capital account and I find no fault with that. I laid down that principle when I was making my argument, but when it came to replace the cars you had in the beginning of 1906, at the beginning of 1907-1908 I claim that you did not make the replacement and that your stock was depreciated by nearly $800,000. Those are facts the minister cannot get away from.
But you have gone back in your traffic.
That is only in the last few months, and so has the Grand Trunk Railway.

The Minister of Railways, when he made his annual statement to the House, spoke of the claims department, and said it was the intention of the department, as I understood him, to reorganize that department of the service.

Is there any further statement to be made on that subject?

The reason I made that statement as to the claims department is that an amendment was moved to the law applied to the government railway, bringing accidents occurring on that road more into line with those on ordinary railways, so far as claims are concerned. But I have heen so busy since the session opened that I have not been able to do what I intended in regard to the matter. Sly bon. friend (Sir. Crocket) will see that it opens up a new avenue as to suits to be taken against the government, for the evidence needed under the old Act was considerably different from that under the new. Sly lion, friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), I think it was, brought in an amendment that has gone through the Senate, and, in face of that, I thought we would have to reorganize the claims department. I intend to pay some attention to the matter later on.

Something certainly ought to be done, because if a person has a claim It is apt to be referred to the claims department at Moncton, and it is months before one seems to be able to get an answer from that office. I think the minister ought to put men in there who know their business. The men who are in there may know their business, but if so they are very dilatory.

At the time to which I refer the minister also stated that he expected to be able to make an announcement to the House with respect to a number of claims standing against the department at the time. I understood that there were many claims concerning which there was no liability under the law as it stood before the amendwent to which the minister referred, but which he proposes to open in view of the change of the law, and that he expected before the end of the season to submit a proposal to parliament for their settlement.
I do not know that I would quite call it an * announcement.' I have been looking into these claims for accidents along the line, cattle killed and that kind of thing.
People injured?
Baggage lost?

The baggage lost comes under another department and we are trying to reorganize that. Since I made my brief statement in the House, I have received innumerable claims. I am having these compiled. All of them, possibly, will not be good, but some of them may. Looking at it from a financial standpoint, my personal view is in favour of not standing upon the technicalities of the law in these matters. If some person has suffered loss, and it is the government's fault, the gov-323
eminent ought not to shield itself behind the technicality. That is the way I feel about it. When 1 have these claims compiled and am able to size up the list, I shall be in a better position to make a statement.
Who is in charge of the claims department?
Freight claims-Mr. Cameron.
But there is an officer called, I think, ' chief claims agent ' ; has there been an appointment made to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Allan?'
Mr. Layton is doing the work temporarily; there lias been no permanent appointment.
Is Mr. Layton a lawyer? Or what qualifications does he possess for the performance of these duties?

I hope my hon. friend will not think I am trying to be facetious about lawyers. I understand that the gentleman is not a lawyer. I may be wrong, but I think that in the settlement of claims such as these, in nine times out of ten, a little practical, hard-headed sense is better as a means of settlement that expert legal knowledge-though the two together would be good.
They do not generally go together.

I would hardly go so far as that. But I have perhaps a peculiar idea as to the settlement of these things.
I think that a shrewd business man who is in touch with the conditions would be as competent as a legal man to settle these claims.
Is it not a fact that the department requires legal advice for the proper settlement of all claims.
In case of a question of legal liability, we have a law branch of our department, and that is referred to as a general thing.
When was Mr. Layton appointed?	.
A couple or three months ago, I think.
At what salary?
I have not the figure before me. I think it is a little less than that of the former occupant of the office. 1 will give the information to-morrow.
Is this the same gentleman who was business manager of the St. .Tohn 'Sun ?'
I am sure I do not know.
Where did he reside ?- what county was he taken from?
I understand he lived in Woodstock.

I would like to ask the minister once more in regard to a point about which I have been inquiring for six months-the connection of the Intercolonial with the Quebec Central at Levis. I do not want to annoy the minister about this, but I think he should take the subject into consideration as well as any other. I have been waiting six months and I think I ought to have a reply and that some action ought to be taken in the matter.
Has that occurred lately ?
Probably in January.

We took the matter up then, and I am informed that the superintendent issued orders that when the Quebec Central Railway was ahead of the mari-tice express it should run into Lfivis and not be detained at Harlaka Junction. That does away with his complaint.

Of course with the curtailment of business on the railway, a large number of men have had to be laid off on the Intercolonial, as on other roads. -conductors, engineers, brakesmen and others. Conductors who have been on the road for years are put back to braking, brakesmen are put back on specials, and special men are laid off. We all admit that when business is poor, we have to curtail, but I do not think it fair that this curtailment should be confined to these men. If my memory serves me right, some years ago when the business of the railway increased considerably, a large number of officials were added, and I think that if this rule is to work for the one class, it should be made to work for the both. If you have to lay off the working men, you should lay off some of the petty officials whom you put on when business is good. All i" ask is a square deal for the man who draws a small salary and that you should lay off some of the officials who are still drawing full pay

and travelling about at the country's expense.
What officials should be laid off?
I can take the book and tell you some.
How many officials are there in the claims branch ?
I do not seem to have the information here.
Can he say what proportion of this sum he is asking for to-day is for wages?

I gave a while ago the amount of the working expenses for 1907, as something over $4,000,000. We have not got the details. I have not got a complete list of the employees. When you come to working expenses, it is like an office staff running a business. You have a certain staff, and if the work declines, perhaps you could do it for a little less, but you have to keep your organization intact.
Who is the inspector of coal and what are his duties?
I cannot tell who he is.
The one I have in mind was a barber. Why can he not be laid off and some engineer appointed who knows more about coal than a barber does?
Engineers are a highly paid class of men, and I imagine they would not care to take a position of that kind.
Is the department putting on the Ocean Limited this summer, between Halifax and Montreal?
The Ocean Limited is not altogether encouraging so far as traffic is concerned, but we expect to put in on about July 5.
Have you an inspector of stationery now?
I think there is no person bearing that title.

I think there was one. I itliink it was necessary to get rid of the gentleman who was purchasing agent, and a new position was created called the inspector of stationery, and this gentleman was appointed thereto. The position carried with it I think $2,000 a year.
That office is abolished, and the occupant is enjoying the benefits of the provident fund organized by the men.
Why was that important office created, and why was it abolished?

That is a matter of ancient history, and I cannot tell. It was created and abolished some time before I came on the scene. I suppose it was 3234
abolished because the office was no longer required.

Would that mean that all the stationery that was going to be required the next ten years was bought under this gentleman's regime? I cannot understand why the situation was created, just what an inspector of stationery had to do. An hon. gentleman here suggests that there was an inspector of window washing. There are inspectors of all sorts of things, particularly about election times. The minister must not shelter himself behind the fact that he has only recently joined the 'department.
I want to place that straight. I have never done that and never will. The hon. gentleman should not make that insinuation.

I was not saying it in any harsh way, I was saying in a very good natured way, because one could scarcely be ill natured with the minister, he is the very soul of good nature himself. Now it does seem to me that we ought to have a little more information with respect to the need for the creation of this office. When we have a list of these different officials, I think we will find others quite as remarkable as that of inspector of stationery and inspector of window washing. I hope the minister will not fail to bring down a list, with the full titles of the different officers.

The minister told us this afternoon, in reply to a question with respect to keeping accounts, that it was impossible for him to give the latest monthly receipts and expenditures. He could give the receipts, but it was impossible to give the expenditures for the month of April and the month of May, implying that it took a long period of time to get in the returns. Now I suppose the system of the Intercolonial is kept on the modern railway basis. I understood that the Intercolonial to-day claims that it has just as good form of accounts, just as up to date a system, as the great railways in the United States and Canada. Take the Canadian Pacific railway for instance. The minister knows that the weekly earnings and expenses of the Canadian Pacific railway are given out, and we find them in the financial and trade papers. I do not think it is more than ten days after the expiry of the week when you find a statement of the Canadian Pacific Railway expenditures and income for the week. I suppose that probably about ten days elapse after the end of the week before the statement is published. Now what is there to prevent the minister of the Intercolonial from giving these statements not longer than ten days after expiration of the week? And especially, what is to prevent him from giving us the April statement now. on the 9th June, or the May statement, on the 9th of June? Under a new minister

and under a practically new deputy we had got the idea that we were going to get the Intercolonial run on the very best basis possibly in the matter of accounting and the strictness with which the accounts are kept. What is the difficulty that the minister finds in not being able to give us weekly statements if we ask for them ten days from the end of the week?
We can give you weekly statements of the earnings of the road.
And of your expenditure?

I am not sure that my hon. friend is right as to a weekly statement of the expenditure. But we can give the weekly earnings. The routine is this : The pay-rolls are not all returned from the different places to the head office at Moncton until after the 15th of the month. We lay down the rule that we must have the returns of the last month on the 25th of the following month. I can give the hon. gentleman the statement for April, and I can give him the statement for May on the 25th June.
It takes twenty-five days after the end of the month before you receive the exact statement of the expenditures here at the office?
This is the head office in a way, and it is not the head office.
Well, at the minister's office ?
Yes.

And it is impossible under your regulations to get this statement sooner unless you urge your officials outside to accelerate their operations by a number of days which would bring it so many dayis sooner to the minister. It seems to me that with your continuous system twenty-five days is a long 'while to wait to get in your returns of the expenditures.
It might possibly be done in la1 shorter time by hiring a larger staff, but I am told that the Grand Trunk system is the same.
What is your pay-day?
The fifteenth.

What has the department been doing, within the last two years, in relation to the reorganization of its system of accounting so as to put the Intercolonial Railway on exactly the same basis as the great railways of the United States?
I am informed that our system of accounting is now the same as that of the great railways of the United States.

I took the trouble a few months ago to get all the reports of the commission in the United States, and I read over the interesting bulletins published as Mr. FOSTER.
to how they have gradually gone about the work of getting a proper system of accounting in order that every species of expense might be definitely set out, each under its owm heading, and I may say it was most interesting though it was a laborious process. They have co-operated with the railway companies themselves. They have not gone on the assumption that they had all the wisdom that enabled them to adopt a form of accounting and have it absolute from the first. They blocked out their system, got into communication with the railway association of the United States and between the two of them they have passed this series of suggestions and propositions, both working loyally together, the commission stating that the railways have co-operated with them splendidly and with the utmost loyalty. But, wThen you come up to the end of it, what they propose to get at is that the wayfaring shareholder may know, from the reports of a railway company, just whether it is acting loyally in the way of allocating its expenses; first, to get what is to be charged to maintenance out of revenue, what, if anything, is to be charged to maintenance out of capital, what new work may properly be charged to revenue and what new work may and must be charged to capital. With reference to the exact percentage of depreciation they have not arrived at the present time, at a scientific method of calculating the amount but that is what they are all working up to, as I understand it. A government railway has this constant temptation; there is a bag always near by into which the minister may dip his hand and consequently there is not the same carefulness in keeping the proper proportion of the charges for the maintenance of the road out of revenue, and there is a constant temptation to make a good showing to parliament by endeavouring to take expenditures of this kind out of one category and put them into another. I am glad to hear the minister say this afternoon that they were trying gradually to get this matter into such a position on the Intercolonial Railway that they may eliminate any doubt as to the plan of accounts, and so that we can all know whether an expenditure for maintenance is charged properly to revenue and that expenditures are only charged to capital when they should be charged to capital. I hope that the minister will persevere in that until we get to the time when the two men on the opposite sides of the House can go to the railway accounts and satisfy themselves that the thing is actually being done on a business basis and that, there is no attempt to charge expenditures to capital which should be charged to revenue. Am T right in saying that the great railways of the United States lay down practically this rule? The building of this road is charged to capital, the interest on construction while it is being built, is charged

to capital, the equipment is charged to capital; the road is not running, there is nothing coming in and there is nothing else to charge it to but to capital. Now, the road is finished on a certain date. You have paid for the road, your station houses, your terminals, your side-tracking and your rolling stock out o*f capital. From that time on every breakage in the rolling stock, the wear and tear of the road must be made good out of the revenue of the road. Am I right in that or not ? If I am wrong then the fundamental position needs to be revised . but that is what J have got from my reading and I believe it to be at the present time the rule of all the great roads. Will the minister tell me if I am right in that ?

I have been reading up this subject myself as my hon. friend will understand and I have learned something about It. The companies do not pretend to try to maintain any number of cars, but they are aiming at maintaining the tonnage of their rolling stock.
In efficiency?

In efficiency, practically. My hon. friend was talking about the number of cars, but you cannot discuss it from the point of view of the number of cars, because the cars that may be built are very much larger than Ithe cars they displace. The idea is to keep up the efficiency and tonnage.

Very well, we will consider the matter according to that. Therefore the road has to have a percentage of the different classes of rolling stock put on each year out of revenue sufficient to keep up the efficiency. The minister is right in that. You might have three box cars one year and you might have next year a box car which has double the capacity. You may double the efficiency by increasing the power of your locomotives but all depreciation must be met out of the revenue of the road, so as to keep it up to its standard efficiency. If you require rolling stock for additional mileage of road that goes to capital unless you have abundant revenue and you wish to take it out of revenue. If there is great increase of traffic the extra rolling stock to accommodate it is taken out of capital, but out of revenue must be taken what is necessary to maintain its efficiency after you procure it. That is the proper principle and the minister has failed to show that he conducts his road on that scientific basis. The minister has also failed to show the House that he took sufficient out of the revenues of the road to maintain its efficiency by providing for loss and depreciation. It would be the best thing that could happen the railway if the policy I have set out were rigorously adhered to, and that no matter what the deficit should be that the minister could show what the
railroad actually costs us. That has not been done in the past. The minister would have the support of the country if he put his railway on that basis even if he faced a deficit which he would explain to the country so that the country might come to a conclusion as to what wa j Dest to do.

In the Auditor General's Report page W-37 there is an expenditure of $5,406.90, for Mr. Schreiber and engineers in connection with the National Transcontinental Railway western division, and amongst other items there is $261 for supplies for the private car of Mr. Schreiber. What has the government got to do with paying expenses on the National Transcontinental Railway western division ?

The government guarantees the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific for the western division and we have an inspecting engineer with his staff to see that the road is constructed up the standard, and on his report the securities are released by the government to the company. This is for the pay of Mr. Schreiber and his staff.
Does the Transcontinental Railway reimburse the government for this outlay ?
We have to undertake this work for our own defense to see that the contract is properly carried out.
Can the minister now tell me how many locomotives were purchased in the year ending 31st March, 1908?
I do not remember that any were purchased but I know some were delivered. I will get the information later.
Is the minister reducing the grades on the Intercolonial Railway to a modern standard ?
All we have recently done is where we are double tracking from Moncton to Painsec junction. Of course the question of reducing the grades is a very important one.
It is absolutely necessary.
We have some large grades but it is a big question and one which concerns the solution of the transpollution problem.

I see by the Auditor General's Report that $3,751,094 were expended in purchasing supplies for the Intercolonial Railway during the year, and in looking over the names of those who supply these goods I can find none who are not politically the friends of the present government. It may be considered fair bv the government to buy exclusively from their political friends, but I think it may be looked upon that it is not entirely a just method
101S7

of conducting business in connection 'with a railway which belongs to the people of Canada as a whole and not to the people of one political party. Among those expenditures I find quite a large amount for advertising, but the advertisements appear to be published only in papers supporting the present government. Even if it was considered that the Intercolonial Railway was a fair pasture for the supporters of the government to feed in, what sort of business sense is there in confining the advertising of excursions and the time tables of the intercolonial Railway, which are for the purpose of inducing as many people as possible to travel by that road, in papers going to only one-half of the people ? If these excursions, for instance, have not been as largely patronized as might be desired, I think it is partly the fault of those in charge of the railway owing to this method of advertising. If there is any reason for this I would like the minister to explain it, but if not, I would be glad to see him make a change from a system which I think is inexcusable from every point of view.

I would be glad to have this item passed before six o'clock, but I might say I have been for some time thinking over the question of advertising which is larger than it looks. In connection with the Intercolonial Railway it is more important to my mind than some other things, although I may be nartial in that respect. I intend before very long to look into the question of advertising; I have not had time to do it yet.
Who is the purchasing agent of the Intercolonial Railway?
Mr. Taylor.
What is his salary?
$135 per month.

I would suppose that it would be his duty to purchase direct from the factories or the wholesalers and not the middlemen, but I find quite the contrary to be the case.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock. ,

Before six o'clock the minister commenced to give some explanation *of his policy with regard to expenditure on the Intercolonial, especially in connection with the advertising. I took the opportunity to bring to his notice that even in the matter of time tables, excursions and things of that kind, the public were not properly notified, and consequently the Intercolonial lost a good deal of patronage. I was in hopes that when a man from Ontario was made a minister, the Intercolo-Mr. DANIEL.
nial would be carried on more as a business proposition and not be so entirely a part of the political machine as it had been. I looked for a considerable change in many respects, more especially in the manner of giving contracts and making expenditures. Take this small matter of advertising, there is absolutely no excuse why these advertisements should not be made general. Surely the minister does not want us to think that the Intercolonial management does not really want the money of Conservatives to help to cut down the deficit. The mode in which these things are carried on-advertising in such a way as to only reach one half of the people-would lead one to conclude that the management do not want the other half to travel on the railway or have any connection with it. The minister ought to let us know whether we can really hope that there will be a change in the future and that the Intercolonial will be run more on a business basis. I am not saying that this government is alone to blame in this connection, but there must be a change somewhere sometime if that railway is to be managed as it ought to be. I shall be glad to have a statement from the minister of the policy he intends following.

I did not have the floor when the House rose, but as regards supplies, they are purchased by tenders at present. The policy is to accept the lowest tender, but there is a great deal of myth about this newspaper advertising for tenders and giving the contract to the lowest. If I were a business man, running the Intercolonial or the Canadian Pacific Railway or Grand Trunk, I would not feel myself bound to accept the lowest tender in every case, but in many cases I would go out in the open market, and in nine times out of ten make a better bargain. If I had a building to put up I would do, as other railway managers do, get it put up by a contractor, who had given me proof of his competence and thoroughness, and not necessarily advertise for the lowest tender. It is necessary however for the government to advertise in the case of these large works. That is the system we have adopted and to which we adhere, but a great deal can be said against the acceptance of the lowest tender being an absolute safeguard.

It is an easy matter in this day for any man to know, when tenders are submitted, whether they are reasonably low or not. It must be apparent to any one, who has to do with public works, that those who tender frequently act in collusion and put up the prices very high. Just look at our contracts for

dredging. It must be apparent to any one who knows anything of the cost of dredging, that many of the contracts are entirely too high. Any intelligent engineer knows whether these tenders are too high or not, and the government is not bound to accept any, even the lowest tender, if it is not a reasonable one. Provided however the government exercise proper diligence, the acceptance of the lower tender is the best policy. Accepting the lowest tender is not always a guarantee that good value is had. The tenderers may be in collusion to raise prices, or, for that matter, there may be only one tender. You avoid the difficulty by employing an agent, but, if you pay a commission, as you have done in the case of some land purchases of from forty to sixty per cent, or if you purchase through such an agent as Merwin, who bought goods at a profit to himself of fifty to seventy-five per cent, of course, you are not getting good value for the money. The minister would be much safer if he sent out an intelligent man to buy in the open market at the best value he could get-he could buy better and cheaper than the government can. But, unfortunately, the government relies upon the plea of having accepted the lowest tender, which, often, is only an excuse for great extravagance. Whether the government can or cannot lay down a hard and fast rule that they will buy by tender only, at least they can give a better example of the way business should be done than many of the instances we have had in the last few years in the purchase of supplies for the Intercolonial.

Are the accounts kept in such a way that the minister can tell us the expenditure on coal month by month? For instance, what value of coal 'has been used for the months of January, February, March, April and May of this" year?
You might as well put in June.
I am not asking as to the particular date, but whether the books are so kept that the expenditure month by month can be shown?
Yes. Take, for instance, the month of March, say
February and March say.
I have the figures for March only. The amount spent for coal for passenger engines was $32,068.87 and for coal for freight engines $114,332.92.
Can the minister tell me what was the expenditure for March of last year?
It was : Coal for freight engines, $81,054.18, and coal for passenger engines, $29,418.15.
There seems to be an increase of about $36,000 or $37,000 for this year. But I understood there was less traffic this year than last.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken; we had a slight increase in March -an oasis in the desert.

I think it would be interesting if the minister would bring down a statement showing the amount of coal used each month from January last up to the end of May, giving comparisons with the same months last year and with figures also showing the comparison of the tonnage of freight hauled. I am advised that the coal bill of this year has been very much in excess of that of last year and that this is largely accounted for-of course, I cannot say that I know this, for I am not a railroad man-by the fact that the road bed is not kept in first-class condition and that the engines have not been in shane to steam. That is, I am told the money of the country is wasted because the railway has not been kept in shape.

On pages W-143 and 144 of the Auditor General's Report, I find charges for legal services by several gentlemen amounting in the aggregate to quite a large sum, having reference to the arbitration with the Grand Trunk Railway with regard to the amounts which may be due to the Intercolonial from the Grand Trunk. So far as my memory goes, we have never had a statement of the results of that arbitration. If so, I think it is only right that the minister should give us the facts and state what amount has been received.

This matter is still before the arbitrators, of course. It involves the question of the adjustment of freight, maintenance, &c. There were several cases before the board of arbitration when Judge Ivillam died. We had expected that the two arbitrators would select a third arbitrator in place of Judge Killam, but they have not done so yet. Speaking roughly, and on information, I may say that the board of arbitrators has laid down certain principles on which further readjustments have been made. Several decisions have been given, and I think on the whole the government has benefited by the awards in its favour to the extent of a balance of between $30,000 and $40,000.
Have the Grand Trunk Railway paid anything over?
They have paid some of these items. There are .other items before the board for adjustment, but they cannot be adjusted until another arbitrator is selected in the place ot the late Judge Killam.

On page 142 there seems to have been a large amount of money paid to the Grand Trunk Railway by the Inter-

colonial, especially at Montreal. Has tlie Intercolonial no employees in Montreal? Do the Grand Trunk employees do all the cleaning of the cars and things of that kind? It would appear so, from the charges that are placed here: Cleaning trucks, cleaning sleepers, parlour cars and ordinary cars, and things of that kind. I also see quite a large amount paid to the Graud Trunk Railway for Grand Trunk cars, I suppose, that have been smashed or damaged on the Intercolonial; but I do not see any contra account of a payment made by the Grand Trunk and other railways for cars belonging to the Intercolonial that have been similarly damaged. Take into consideration the large number of Intercolonial cars that are scattered all over the country on other railways, I should think there ought to he some revenue from that source, as well as an expenditure by the Intercolonial for that purpose.

We pay $140,000 a year to the Grand Trunk for running rights over their line from Ste Rosalie to Montreal, paying in proportion to the expense for maintenance. They supply the men. If any of our cars are broken by other lines, we collect from them, as they collect from us.
Is the Railway Department buying any coal from_the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company this year?
I think some coal is being taken from that company.
I see last year you bought 356 tons from that company. Where is the bulk of the coal bought for the operation of the railway?

We buy from several coal companies, from the Cumberland, Springhill, Maritime, Inverness, Dominion, Nova Scotia, and several companies in New Brunswick. The price is a little higher than it was last year.

I see an item of $16,000 for advertising. I understand that it came out in an investigation before the committee that the papers in which the government advertised are all of one shade of politics. May I ask the minister if he proposes to continue that policy, or does he propose to broaden it a little?
We discussed the question of advertising before six o'clock. The whole question is one which I intend to take up, hut I am not prepared to say what I shall do until I see what the conditions are.

Does the minister still pursue the same line of advertising the railroad by means of pictures and displays at different exhibitions throughout the country, showing the beautiful scenery along the route of the Intercolonial; and is there an Mr. DANIEL.
officer employed for that purpose by the railway ?
We have done something of that kind. We had a very good display at the automobile show, both in Toronto and in Montreal. I think the Creighton Advertising Department is in charge of that.
Have you an advertising department?
We have a traffic manager, under whom Mr. Creighton attends largely to the advertising.

The minister says he proposes to take this matter up for consideration, and if he is going to I.eave the impression upon the public that there is no politics iir the management of the Intercolonial we shall expect that some of these advertisements will appear in Conservative newspapers. I have before me a long list of newspapers with a very small circulation, but containing advertisements of the government, while papers with three times the circulation in the same city and town, are omitted. I would like to remind the minister that it would be rather difficult for him to make the Canadian people believe that there are no politics in the management of the Intercolonial Railway, when, in putting an advertisement into a newspaper, he selects the one having a small circulation and allows the one having a large circulation to go without any advertisement whatever. I hope the minister will investigate this matter, keeping this point before him and that next year, when we see this large list of newspapers receiving pretty large amounts of money, we will find that advertisements have been published in the newspapers having a large circulation. Perhaps the minister might indicate what he proposes to do on that point. I do not think that it requires very much investigation.
I have made a statement, three times, twice in reply to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and once in reply to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) concerning that.

It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to say that he proposes to look into this matter in the days to come. Surely the hon. gentleman would not require very much time to indicate to the House what he proposes to do on a question of this kind. The minister has not much faith In his own policy with respect to asking for public tenders. He suggests that if he would apply his own mind to the subject he would not ask for tenders in many cases at all. Yet, my hon. friend knows that the people believe that tenders should be asked for. The policy that my hon. friend adopts in putting a number of reformers on the list and handing them a slip asking for ten-

ders is a policy that does not involve the principle of inviting public tenders at all. It is a political policy adopted by the minister for the [DOT]purpose of distributing public patronage among his political friends. My bon. friend understands that. He has had a wide experience in Ontario and, having brought that experience with him. and, I suppose, having profited by the result, I was very much surprised that he should adopt the same policy in the new office he has been selected to occupy. I do not think it will appeal to the minister's good judgment to say that after being several months in the department he would come forward and, on these two points, put himself in opposition to the Canadian people, by saying, with respect to the question of pffblic advertisement, that, if his own opinion were to prevail he would not ask for tenders at all simply going to his own friends and allowing them to put up a building costing $25,000 or $30,000 because they happened to be in the business. He would not give a Conservative in. any part of Canada any opportunity whatever to tender for the construction of any public work. These are matters that it would not take my bon. friend a very long time to decide. The only answer is that he must be careful of the interests of his party before he comes to a decision. My hon. friend, who wants to lead in the expenditure of money is not willing to adopt the policies which are adopted by smaller institutions and organizations throughout the country because he says he would not, if he had his own way, ask for tenders at all.
May I ask the minister whether he accepts the lowest tender in purchasing concrete pipes ?
The department accepts the lowest tender in every case unless some reason can be shown why It should not do so.

Would the minister be good enough to give us some reason why he did not accept the lowest tender in connection with concrete piping. I asked a question on the 13th April and I had the answer of the minister forwarded to parties who tendered. I will just quote a few words from a letter I received in reply :
If you compare the prices our is much more favourable, without any discount, but when you deduct 15 per cent I certainly should have had the contract.
This is a most reliable firm. They sent in their tender and their tender was not only lower than the figures which the contract was let for but in addition to that they were willing to take off 15 per cent and they did not receive the contract.

My hon. friend will remember that he is warned every day, with respect to the sale of patent medicines, not
to take anything that he is told is just as good. The pipe tendered for in this instance was not the kind that the specification called for. Our engineer of maintenance of ways reported that the other pipe was the pipe we wanted. That Is why we did not take it.

Was it because you wanted Wallberg to supply it ?
Mr, GRAHAM. My hon. friend, with his usual wisdom, does not know that it was not Mr. Wallberg at all who is interested in this contract.

I do not think that is a satisfactory answer. I am well aware that these people put in a tender in the same way as the others were put in and that they were ready and willing to manufacture these goods under any specification that was proposed to them. There is nooccasion for the minister to make the statement he has made in that regard.

I assure my hon. friend that the goods are purchased always from the lowest tenderers unless there is some good reason given to the contrary. I am not so wedded to the tender system, as my hon. friend seems to be, and which he regards as a panacea for everything, as to say that I will take something that I do not want, but I will get the full particulars for my hon. friend and I think he will find that there is no reason for complaint on behalf of his friends.

How can the minister state that the lowest tenders are always accepted when here we have a most reliable company which is not only the lowest tenderer, but which offered 15 per cent off the tender price in addition, and yet it did not get the contract ? I notice from the reply given by the minister in ' Hansard ' that this Kemptville Company has been supplying a large quantity of concrete piping for two years. How can he condemn the concrete piping of the other companies when he has made no endeavour to compare one with the other.
I am not condemning the quality of the piping of any other firm. We wanted a flat bottom piping and they offered us round piping.	.

I do not believe that is a sufficient excuse for the minister to throw away the people's money as he has done. This firm if it were given a chance could have supplied the department with flat bottom piping at a great deal less cost than he paid to the other firm.

As to the tiling, the hon. gentleman is no doubt speaking from a letter he has in his possession. He evidently knows something of the tile business but not enough to form a correct judgment in reference to it. We wanted flat bottomed piping which is the more expensive of

the two and this firm offered us round piping.
Were tenders called for flat bottom piping?
I imagine they were. The engineer recommended flat bottom tiling and we took it from the Kemptville people on tender and there Is nothing extraordinary1 about it.
I am informed that this company to which I refer sent in their application in accordance with the tender.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) know whether this company tendered for round or for flat bottomed pipe ?
As I understand it they tendered for the pipe called for by the department. '

I put in several thousand tons of this piping last year and I am very familiar with the business. I know that flat bottom concrete pipe for railway culverts will cost from 10 to 20 per cent more according to the size than the round pipe costs. All the railway engineers and the municipal engineers for sewage pipe insist on flat bottom pipe for sizes between 24 and 30 inches in diameter because it will stand a greater strain than the round pipe. It is absurd to say one kind of pipe is the same as the other. The Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Northern all use flat bottom pipe. If the hon. gentleman can tell me the size and what they were bidding on I can show the absurdity of his position if he claims that round pipe is the same as flat bottomed pipe.

This firm has several branches in Canada and in the United States and they are a responsible firm and are in the habit of furnishing the material for railway and municipal work. I know these men and I am satisfied they would not tender for round pipe if the tender called for flat bottomed pipe and they say they complied with the tender.

According to the Auditor General's Report, T. McAvity & Sons, of St. John, N.B., were paid $27,896.40 last year for supplies for the Intercolonial Railway. Were tenders asked for the supply of this hardware?
Oh, yes, in every case.
By public advertisement or by circulars to those on the patronage list ?
I am informed by circular to a very large number of people.
What other firms were invited to tender for this hardware ?
I am told there are somew'here in the vicinity of 75 names on the list altogether.
Were 75 other firms invited to tender for that hardware ?
I imagine they would be, all the hardware firms we had the names of.
Was any other firm at St. John invited to tender ?
I could not say.

Would the McAvity firm be the only one in New Brunswick that would be invited to tender ?
Mr. fillAITAM. I think not, but I cannot say as I am not conversant with the location of the different firms.
What is it necessary for a man to do in order to get on the patronage list ? My hon. friend from Toronto says a good subscription to the election fund.
He knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is thinking of the old days.

He will not be better informed than the minister himself because he has had experience in these matters. The minister says there is public advertisement, but when we come to the point we find there is a list of friends and when goods are required those on that list are notified and they are asked to give prices to the department.
My hon. friend has said that I said there was public advertisement. I was perfectly frank with my friend from Fredericton, and said they were asked by circular.
I said that my hon. friend was trying to leave the impression that these goods were purchased after public advertisement, and then he tried to qualify it.
I did not try to qualify it, I made no qualification. My hon. friend should not repeat that when he knows I did not say it.
It is no use trying to suggest to the House that my hon. friend is purchasing goods after public advertisement by tender. What qualification must a man have to get on the list ?

My hon. friend is not nearly so childlike and bland as he pretends. He is one of the strongest partisans in the Dominion of Canada ; he bends every energy to that point and I do not blame him, and yet he wants the House to

believe be is so innocent that he does not know anything about government patronage and never heard of such a thing in his life. He knows that so long as governments are in power in this or any other country and are run on the party system, so long will there be a slight tendency for the government in power, whether Liberal, Conservative or Independent, to have, to use an old phrase, a slight cant so far as their friends are concerned. That is the case with all the provincial governments and every government wWre the party system is in force. What the country first demands and is interested in is that we get value for our money, not that goods be bought from my hon. friend's friends. When we ask a dozen or more good firms to compete and they do compete and we buy at the lowest price, I think it can be taken that we have received good value.

In this case I question whether more than one firm were asked to tender, for if more firms in New Brunswick were asked to tender. I do not believe that McAvity & Sons would succeed in every case in getting the order. What other firms in New Brunswick were invited?
I can bring the list tomorrow, but I am sorry to say I cannot give the names as I am not familiar with the locations.
I am speaking of the firms in New Brunswick. T. McAvity & Sons and McLean, Holt & Company are practically the same firm.

I see that L. S. Macoun, of Ottawa, who last year sold $74,000 worth of goods to the Militia Department, is now working into the Railway Department. He has been selling wooden water buckets, varnish brushes, fire-clay and lead pipe and managed to get from the Railway Department on stores account last year, $182.31. He, I understand, is very closely connected with a member of the government, and I had his own statement the other day that he did not keep a shop olfactory and had no supplies of his own to sell. I take it therefore that this is another case of the Intercolonial Railway buying from a middleman. It occurred to me that Wallberg had better be looking after himself when I found Macoun figuring in the Railway Department on stores account as well as in the Militia Department. I would like to ask the minister if tenders were asked for these goods supplied by Mr. Macoun.
Tenders no doubt were asked for and the lowest accepted.
Is Mr. Macoun on the list?

He seems to be on that list. This confirms what nine out of ten business men will agree to, and that is that calling for tenders is not a panacea for everything. It is the only thing parliament will allow a minister to do, but it is not always the best way. Speaking of middlemen, ask for tenders for some item, and you will find the manufacturer giving you a tender higher than that made by a middleman, who is his agent, tendering for the same goods. You ask how that is. They give the agent a commission and he divides his commission. It is cheap.er for the government, by the tender system, to buy from the agent' often than from the manufacturer himself.
That has not been shown in the Public Accounts Committee.
I can show cases time and again in my department in which the original manufacturer has tendered at a higher price than his agent for the same goods.
You forget about Mer-win.
I was speaking generally. It may seem heresy to say that the tender system is not-always the best, but that is the experience of business men on many occasions.
Did the company advance Mr. Macoun the money before the goods were delivered as was done in the case of the copper purchase?
I do not know to what my hon. friend refers when he speaks of the copper purchase. No money is advanced by this department.

It is singular that the minister does not know about the copper purchase, but he has been so taken up with the little matter in Brockville that he has not had time to keep himself posted on what is going on in the committees. This copper transaction
