I forgot-there is our censor again. But surely, Mr. Chairman, you will not refuse me the opportunity of giving the Minister of Railways much needed information. I would be most happy to inform him what I meant by the transaction in copper, but I must bow to the decision of my hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Ross) as expressed through you, Mr. Chairman.
That is the first sensible thing you have done to-day.
I see another firm here which has been supplying blankets and towels and things of that kind called the Peter McSweeney Company of Moncton. Is that the senator of that name?

I do not know whether it is or not.
Mr. DANIEL,, it is a good deal like his name anyway.
I also notice an account of Macfarlane & Thompson. The Minister of Railways seems to be buying from that firm. That is the firm of which Senator Thompson is a member.

This is dangerously close to a violation of the Independence of Parliament Act. I think the party has done well enough by these senators by giving them a seat for life with a salary of $2,500 a year. Still you continue to load them with benefits by putting them on the patronage list. That is rather unfair to the rest of your supporters. There are other firms which have Liberal leanings as well as the firms of Peter McSweeney and Macfarlane & Thompson. I think that for the services rendered his country Mr. Mc-Sweene.v was too well paid by putting him in the Senate and I can say the same of Senator Thompson. You put these gentlemen in the Senate, a position to which one would rather be surprised that they would even aspire to, and yet you are not satisfied with that but you put them on the patronage list and give them a large amount of patronage, thus enabling them to make, in addition to their large salaries which they draw as senators, large profits on the merchandise they sell the various departments of the government. On behalf of the other firms which do give you loyal and honest support, I protest against the minister doing this. He should strike these men off the patronage list. I have no personal conceim in the matter, but am actuated merely by a love of fair play and a square deal.
Was the iron purchased by public tender or private sale?
All the stores are purchased in the same way.
Am I to understand that the large amount of iron purchased, $76,000, page 126-W, and $34,000, page 127-W
From whom ?
From the Nova Scotia Coal and Steel Company and the Portland Rolling Mills.

We buy these supplies from the lowest tenderer, and I am very glad to purchase goods from the Nova Scotia Steel Company or any other Canadian company which is developing our resources. We give them no advantage.
If others are not on the list, as I understand it, then they cau-not possibly tender. Is it possible that contracts for' these large amounts are simply
given to those who are on the patronage list? That is a most outrageous piece of business management.
Carried.

My bon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) would say ' carried ' to anything this government could propose. Just as long as you can get your hand into the public chest and pull out money, it is all right.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Order.
%

Hand it out to party friends and everything is lovely. Here is a contract of about $125,000 handed over to party friends. Does the minister think that is fair and reasonable? Does he say that these large contracts should be open to tender only by parties who are on the patronage list?
The hon. gentleman will not speak of the capital invested in the Nova Scotia Steel Company as Liberal capital?

I am not referring to it as being Liberal capital. But what excuse has the minister for not advertising such contracts as this? Surely, they should be advertised very widely, instead of being open only to a few party friends of the minister.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) allows himself to be led away. He should not feel any sorer than I do. I have been told that I am sore over the result in Brockville, but he should not allow himself to be bad-natured over the result in East Lambton. These things happen to the best of men.
Mr, BLAIN. Not many happened like East Lambton.

But it did happen in East Lambton. We cannot help these calamities. As to this contract being given to a friend of this government, I think the hon. gentleman would hardly venture to call the president of the Nova Scotia Steel Company a friend of this government. If he were to do so, he would get into trouble. It is a good substantial firm, with a good substantial Conservative as its president. But, it being the lowest tenderer, we bought the goods from this company.

But the point is that only those on the list are given the privilege of tendering. As to East Lambton, the hon. gentleman knows that that is one of the ridings in w'hich there is a very considerable overlapping, and the town and township in which I live happened to send something over 400 to add to the majority.
Order.

Hon. gentlemen opposite are very much afraid that we may begin to talk about what happened yester-

day. Certainly, they can take very little satisfaction out of it. But does not the minister think it unreasonable and unbusinesslike for him, in making an expenditure of over $100,000 for such commodities ns iron and steel, that he should not invite tenders widely? Or does he expect to continue to ask tenders from a few political friends?
On this question of
Mr. Chairman I was asking a question of the minister and I think

1 am not going to obstruct; I will give you lots of opportunity to do that. I was about to say: On this question of purchasing supplies, I would like to say a word or two to the minister. But, before doing that, let me address an observation to my hon. friend from East Lambton. He need not get fussy about the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company or any of the large companies doing business in the eastern part of this country ; he will find that they are doing business in a legitimate way and are neither receiving nor asking favours from this government. When the hon. gentleman says that I am content to have this money go into the pockets of party friends, I want to say that the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company is not a party friend of mine. Its warmest friends have never charged it with being a friend of the Liberal government. Its history for twenty years in Nova Scotia has been exactly the reverse. The president of the company is the bell-wether of the Conservative party in Nova Scotia. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) knows that very well. It ill-beeomes any member on that side to charge the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company with receiving undue advantage from any government. There are some of us who might have reasons to complain, but certainly not hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. But, though they are no party friends of mine, or of the government I support, they should receive their legitimate share of the business of the government. I would go so far as to say to the minister that, in a matter of this kind the purchase of bar iron, &c., if there are any preferences to be given, they should go to the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company; and I will tell you why: If my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) will take the trouble to inquire, he will find that this company is one of the best customers the Intercolonial has. I am not aware that they have ever asked for any preference, but I say that if the time ever comes when they do, then, in the interests of the road and of the country as well as of the company, he would be very well justified in giving them the preference.

I do not wish to have words put in my mouth that I did not
use. I did not object to the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, as such, receiving this contract. But, as I understand it, when these supplies are needed, tenders are asked for only from a certain number of firms. There is no reason why the minister should not be able to estimate in advance, more or less accurately, how much of these supplies he is going to need in the course of a year. It seems to me that it is not reasonable that so large a contract for such supplies as these should merely be peddled round, as it were, amongst the minister's party friends.

Was there any competition with the Nova Scotia 'Steel Company with this order? I understood from the minister that there were seventy-five persons on the patronage list who furnish supplies to the Intercolonial. I suppose that out of that seventy-five there was only the Nova Scotia Steel Company who were able to supply the coal. Is the minister certain that there was competition with the Nova Scotia Company for that coal ?
There is no doubt of the competition. As a .matter of fact, we have all the leading firms on the list.
Who awards the contracts?
The contracts are awarded by the minister and his deputy.

There has been a change since I was minister. At that time, unless there was some objection to the material the contracts were awarded by the manager of the Intercolonial, Mr, Pottinger. In case there was a tie, or the material was not up to the standard, the decision was left to the scientific branch of McGill University. In the case of oii, for instance, as to which was the best lubricant, the question was left to the scientists of McGill, who always made a report to the department, and on their report the contract was made. But it never came before the minister unless there was a tie, or some question which the head of the department could alone decide.

I have followed the system adopted by my predecessors, which I think is a right one. It is better to have the tenders sent to the head office for decision. Being myself responsible to the House and to the country, I feel like seeing how the awards are given every time. I can assure my hon. friend that unless there is some good reason for it the contract is always given to the lowest tenderer.
I see you bought a quantity of blankets. What need have you for blankets?
For the sleeping cars.

I see an item here for the Peter McSweeney Company, of which

the chief is Senator McSweeney, He is in fact the whole company, and he has profited to a large extent in the way of supplying blankets, towelling, cotton and flannelettes. What do you do with flannelettes ? Do you make night gowns for the porters, or was it just because there was a desire on the part of the department to give a little patronage to the senator, who is not receiving quite enough in his sessional indemnity? There was a considerable amount of this flannelette, 576$ yards. I think the senator might have thrown in that half yard. It does seem to me that a man occupying so distinguished a position as senator of Canada, should not have charged this government for that half yard. Perhaps the minister will explain what that flannelette was used for.
I imagine it was used in the sleeping cars. It also might possibly be used as cushions for the dining tables.
How about the oil you are buying from the New Brunswick Petroleum Company? Did you buy that oil from the wells, or did you buy it through middlemen?
My information is that it was bought from the producers.
Do you buy your oil in the same way that you buy the flannelette ?
Not by the yard, no.

I mean, do you ask for tenders from certain persons who are upon the list or do you buy in the open market? On page W-147 I see you pay a large sum of money for oil to the Galena Signal Oil Company. Then there is the Imperial Oil Company of St. John, I think that is managed by a good Liberal, the present mayor of the city, Mr. Bullock, who figures largely on this list, some $25,000. Then there is the Keenleyside Oil Company. I presume some of this must be lubricating oil, and some of it crude oil. What do you use the crude oil for?

For forging work, heating rivets. Our lubricating oil is purchased by tender on a guarantee that a certain quantity will serve for a thousand engine miles. The Galena Signal Oil Company has the contract at the present time. I think we got one or two other tenders. One of the things that we are trying to get down to a practical basis is the cost of lubrication per mile. We buy oil on the guarantee of a certain cost, reckoned on the mileage of the locomotive.
Did you buy this lubricating oil on tender open to all the world ?
I think that at one time we had tenders from all the oil companies practically.

Do you ask for tenders
every year ?
There are not a great many oil companies. The Imperial Oil Company of Canada is really a branch of the Standard Oil Company. We made a contract with it for a term of years.
Where is the Galena Oil Company operating ?
It is an American company. I am told that it is practically an offshoot of the Standard Oil Company. It has a branch, I understand, in Toronto.
There are Canadian oil companies. There is the Canadian Oil Company arid the Queen City Oil Company. Why have these not had an opportunity of tendering?

They did have an opportunity. This is the only company that gives the required guarantee. We are reducing the cost of lubrication and we are carrying on a test. These people make a specialty of it and I imagine they are supplying the lubrication for 75 or 90 per cent, of the railways of the continent.

The government should give the preference to the home companies. We have the Queen City, the Canadian Company, and I am told there are other Canadian companies. I do not think you should make a contract for three or four years. Suppose these people were not able, in this particular year, to compete with the American company, perhaps next year they would be able to compete and I think .a contract should be made from year to year so as to give our home companies an opportunity.

There is a peculiar situation. We have to give the contract for a term of years to get a proper price. My hon. friend will see the importance of it both with respect to the rolling stock and the cost of the lubrication itself. This company make a specialty of it and they send a man around on the locomotives and cars to see that the consumption is kept within proper bounds because they have to guarantee the amount of oil we use per mile at a certain price. Canadian companies should have an opportunity to compete and when our contract runs out I would be very glad to give them that opportunity. Everything being equal, I would prefer the Canadian companies under all circumstances.
This is a three or five years contract and unfortunately the minister will not have an opportunity of giving the contract to a Canadian company. It will be in other hands.
My hon. friend may.
But I do not see how any company could possibly send a man on every engine to see that you did not use too much oil.
Not on every engine. They keep a man there a great deal of the time. He is not on every engine but he practically instructs them in the use of oil and keeps his eye on the consumption.

There is a large purchase of iron in the city of St. John from Me-Avity and the McLean Holt Company amounting to $51,213. Do I understand the minister that in buying that iron and ironwork from these two firms, which ax-e practically as I understand it, one firm, every one of the other 74 had an opportunity to put in their price for these goods ?

I think my hon. friend will find, as a matter of fact, that there were quite a number of tenders. My hon. friend speaks of the other 74 ; 1 did not mean to say that there were 74 iron or hardware men, but of the large number that are on the list all that are engaged in that business were, I have no doubt, given an opportunity to tender. We never invite tenders but the Montreal and Toronto men are keen competitors in iron and steel goods. It is not at all likely that these goods were all bought in one purchase. It would be throughout the year and the total would be made up by portions of the different stores purchased.
Is it confined to two firms in St. John ?
All these purchases which are spread over the year are the subject of competition. They would form part of a large amount of stores that were purchased during the year.
These were all the purchases that were made from McAvity ?
I think they would not be bought at one time but on several different occasions.
As I understand it they would be bought in small quantities as they were needed ?
I think so.
What I was trying to make sure of was whether there was any competition or not.
Yes.
For these parcels of goods bought throughout the year Montreal and Toronto iron firms had a chance to compete ?
I think my hon. friend will find that is absolutely true.
Of course, I understand this is confined to persons who are on the patronage list.
Yes.

I notice you have been buying some railway ties from Pearson, B. F., of Halifax. That, I take it, is Mr. B. F. Pearson, sometimes known as the Eastern Supply Company, sometimes as B. F. Pearson, sometimes as Matthew Lodge, sometimes as Henderson, sometimes as the St. John Suu Publishing Company, Limited, sometimes as the Morning ' Chronicle,' Halifax, sometimes as the Glace Bay ' Times,' and sometimes as the Halifax ' Echo.' He has a variety of names ; he appears in a variety of characters. He is in point of fact a lawyer of the city of Halifax and he sells ties-railway ties

not neck ties-but railway ties to the government. I could understand that it might be reasonable for a Senator to sell flannelette if he happened to be in the dry goods business, but why a gentleman of the legal profession would be around peddling hemlock ties to the government is something I canuot understand. This man does not get out these ties, he is not a lumberman, he has no mills, but he is simply in the same position as regards the Intercolonial Railway as Mr. Macoun is in as regards the Department of Militia and Defence and the Intercolonial Railway. Neither of these gentlemen is a producer of anything, neither of them keeps a shop. In fact, as I understand it, one of them was very indignant when he was asked if he kept a shop. He was horror stricken that it would be put up to him for a moment that he would be engaged in such a business as shop-keeper and I suppose that Mr. Pearson would be quite indignant if it were intimated to him he was a shop-keeper or that he kept a retail lumber yard. For the year ending 31st March, 1906, Mr. Pearson sold over $100,000 ties to the government. Under what circumstances were these ties bought from Mr. Pearson of Halifax, lawyer, proprietor of the St. John ' Sun,' Morning ' Chronicle,' the Glace Bay ' Times,' the Halifax ' Echo,' chief push of the Eastern Supply Company, member of the Nova Scotia legislature, and local government; a man of a variety of titles and a variety of occupations and a many sided man, taking him altogether ?

We use nearly 1,000,000 ties a year, and I do not know under what circumstances these particular ties were got. The price has increased materially during the past few years, and one of the greatest difficulties of all railways is to get ties at all. Even if my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) were to offer ties to us I would be prepared to accept them so long as we had not to pay more than the fair market price. We fix the price we will pay for ties and make

all the contracts we can. We care not whether we buy from a professional man or any one else so long as we get them at a fair price. We have refused to purchase ties because too high a price was asked for them. The fact that Mr. Pearson may be called a middleman by my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) would not make any difference to me in the purchase of ties if I got them at a proper value.

Does the minister think one would be straining 'his imagination if he were to suggest that the person who owned these ties thought it necessary in order to sell them to the department to interest Mr. Pearson who seems to have the [DOT]ear of the government ? I fancy that the man who produced these ties has found it necessary to interest Mr. Pearson by the promise of a commission before he was able to make a sale to the government, and I know that the gentleman who did produce them has political views which are not in accord with the administration. I believe that is actually what occurred. The minister has told us that the patronage of the government naturally goes to its political friends. Mr. Pearson is a political friend of the government, but I believe the government has been more of a friend to Mr. Pearson than Mr. Pearson has been to the government, for X do not believe he has returned dollar for dollar that they have him. He certainly did not in the Halifax land case where he made a profit of $28,000 which he divided with his friends, Mr. Pearson's share alone being $14,000. I have no doubt he got a very handsome commission in connection with the sale of these ties, because I know as a matter of fact that the ties were produced by a man who was not in political accord with the government, and he was only able to sell the ties to the government by reason of the fact that he employed Mr. Pearson as a middle man. That is one of the evils of the system -which the Minister *of Railways defends. No man along the line of the Intercolonial Railway who is not a political supporter of the government can sell any material to the railway in any large *quantities.
Mi1. GRAHAM. What about the Nova Scotia Steel Company?

The Nova Scotia Steel Company stands in a peculiar position because they are the largest patrons of the Intercolonial Railway in the matter of freight and the department would make an exception * in their favour, but outside of that and some small things the officers of the department are not allowed to buy from others than political supporters. Here is Mr. S. S. Ryan, who runs a small farm across from Moncton in the county of Albert, who was formerly local member for the county, but he was defeated list Mr. GRAHAM.
election; he sells thousands and thousands of dollars worth of lumber to the Intercolonial which the Intercolonial could buy cheaper from the various mills, but these mill owners being enterprising men they are Conservatives, and therefore they have to sell to the Intercolonial Railway through Mr. Ryan or some other friend of the government. In that way, through political exigencies, the Department of Railways, pays a great more money for all its supplies than it is necessary to pay. That is one reason why the road has to [DOT] be run at a loss. This new minister coming from the province of Ontario he was not governed by local considerations as a minister from New Brunswick would be, and we did hope on the principle that a new broom sweeps clean, that the political management of the road would end and that it would be run as a business proposition, but our hopes have been disappointed. There is no reason in the world why the Intercolonial Railway should not pay as well as any other trunk line in Canada. Along its route are thriving and prosperous towns and productive farms. There is no better country under the sun than that through which the greater portion of the Intercolonial Railway runs. The minister knows that it runs through a splendid country and that throughout the length of the line there is local traffic. The Canadian Pacific Railway, that great trunk road, for 700 or 800 miles has no possibility of any local traffic of any amount being created, and yet the Canadian Pacific Railway is able to make in some years as high as 15 per cent on its capital stock, which was originally, to some extent, watered. The Intercolonial Railway, on the other hand, running through a better average country than the Canadian Pacific Railway, has a deficit as I proved this afternoon, logically, if not to the satisfaction of the minister, of aboht $800,000 on the year's working of the road for 19067. The minister must see that in order to bring about a change in the results he must effect a change in the manner of conducting the road. I advise the minister if he wants to go down in history as one of the best ministers the Intercolonial has had, to make these changes, to apply the pruning knife, to abolish th'e patronage system, to cut out the politics and run the road as a business proposition. If the minister adopts that policy and method, the road, instead of being an annual loss to the exchequer of this country, will pay a handsome dividend upon the capital employed. The minister is young and full of vitality and some brains
In a modified form.

He may not have a long period of office before him but in view of the circumstances of the last few days we will have no election this year so he is at

least sure of another year in office, and if he is industrious and earnest and attempts to accomplish these reforms he will make for himself a reputation such as no other Minister of Railways has made, at least since 1S96.
Mr. jOSLER. I was sorry to hear the minister so strongly defend the patronage system. I thought it. was something which while more or less recognized was still something to be ashamed of. I do not think there is a more corrupting influence in public life than the patronage system as carried on in Canada either by the Dominion or any local government. There is practically no direct purchase, every thing has to go through a middleman, unless the man is on the patronage list. If he quarrels with the government he is at once stricken off the list without question and If he has goods which the government must have they can only be sold to the government through a middleman. You cannot get a contract to carry the troops from Toronto to Niagara except it goes through a middleman. I say what I know. There is no more paralyzing system in the world than the system of the patronage committee and the middleman. I am sure that the minister is himself anxious to do what is absolutely right for the country and his department and I commend to him Lord Cromer's book on ' Modern Egypt,' just published, which is one of the most interesting books that can be read. I sent to the library but it was not there. I regret' that as I would have liked to read to the minister a paragraph from that book. In summing up the reasons why Egypt has been changed from one of the most corrupt countries in the world to one where everything is honestly administered, Lord Cromer says in the chapter headed, ' Corruption,' that one of the chief influences in overcoming corruption was that when the government came under the control of the English a policy was adopted of letting public works and buying supplies by public tender. That one order did more to bring about a reign of honesty in Egypt than all other reforms put together. If this government will only adopt that principle, they will find that the Intercolonial Railway as many other departments, will run smoothly and at once a different tone will be brought into our public life. You cannot have honesty when you have a system of patronage committees and patronage firms from whom you buy ; it is an Impossibility. There must be more or less corruption under such circumstances, and I am sorry to hear the minister so strongly defend the patronage system. I know that this has been more or less the condition under all our governments, local and Dom-324
inion, but I appeal to the minister to see whether he could not change that as far as his department is concerned. If he does so he will deserve the thanks of the whole people, and I ask him to seriously consider the suggestion.

I am sure we all appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) and I hope the minister will take them to heart. What number of commission agents has the hon. gentleman in the United States gathering trade for the railroad ?

We have no agents in the United States. It is a mistake to say that we do not advertise for tenders. Nothing is purchased without tender. The great majority of our goods are bought after advertising in the newspapers. My hon. friend (Mr. Osier)) shakes his head. That is absolutely true so far as the Railway Department is concerned. The stores are purchased in the way I have said. The other materials are purchased after advertising in the newspapers for tenders. I can show my hon. friend the tenders.

I cannot quite understand the minister's statement when he says he has not any one receiving commissions. On W-131 I see that we paid John A. Boak a commission of 10 per cent on securing business, $2,982.
I was in error; we have an agent in Chicago.
Ticket sellers as well have received in the neighbourhood of $2,000 commission on selling tickets. How many of these agents has the minister got?
People who sell tickets always get a commission on them. We have one man in Chicago and I think the other is in Boston. All railroads pay a commission on tickets sold.

I see on page 137 that $2,288 were paid under the heading of association fees. There are the American Railway Association of New York; the Association of American Railway Accounting officers, Chicago ; the Canadian Car Service Bureau, Montreal; the Canadian Freight Association, Toronto; the Master Car Builders Association, Chicago ; the Railway Car Association, Buffalo, the Railway Equipment and Publication Company, New York. Board of trade fees:	Halifax, Moncton, Montreal,
Quebec and Toronto, and sundry association fees. I notice one very serious omission. The Board of Trade at St. John is not mentioned at all and no fees are paid it although it is, I presume, about as important as the majority of the others mentioned. What is the object of these payments and what is gained by them?

Like all railways, we join these associations for the mutual bene-



fit to be derived, such as information interchangeable among members of the association. All railways join these associations. It is necessary for the Intercolonial to join them if it is to keep up with the other railways. We get the standards of cars and equipment and all that kind of thing.
Do they issue publications yearly ?
Yes.
I notice a payment of $1,312 to the Canadian Freight Association of Toronto, being proportion of expenses for nine months. What expenses would those be?

There is some sharing of expenses in connection with that association among the different roads. As to the boards of trade, it seems to be necessary, for the benefit of the railway itself, to encourage the boards of trade in these different places. I do not see why St. John was left out.

I hope the minister will correct that omission, if there is anything to be gained by correcting it at all.
. Mr. FOSTER. I would like to have an explanation of W-161, reconstruction of accounting system, paid to Kenneth Falconer, $26,252.21.

There is a return giving all the information with regard to that. This firm reorganized our system of accounting, not only at the head office but the different smaller places, and I am informed that their work has paid the railway already. For example, take the fixing of cost, although we thought we had a fairly good system, we were unable before to fix anything as definite regarding the cost of mileage and that kind of thing. We had in addition an expert, who was the controller of the Chicago and Rock Island Railway, who gave us some very practical views. I feel confident that we got full value by that reorganization.
How much money was spent on that?
I gave it in the House not long since and it is in ' Hansard.' I think it was in the vicinity of $40,000.
Out of what appropriation was that paid?
Out of working expenses.
Does the minister think that belonged to the working expenses of the railway?
We are charging the account to the working expenses.

Certainly. It is the accounting of your men who are under regular salary for that purpose who are doing Mr. GRAHAM.
it. Here was a special work undertaken by the Intercolonial and you had to pay some $50,000 for it. The country knew nothing about it until the contracts were made and the larger part of the work was done. That illustrates the trouble of having a bulk item of $9,000,000 such as this. It is perfectly possible for the railway department to spend $8,900,000 on one item-advertising, say-and the Auditor General would have no chance to criticise it. This illustration reduces it to an absurdity, but it is only to show what an absolutely blind appropriation this is. On a new arrangement, one not coming up in the ordinary run of the business, the minister committed the country to an expenditure of $50,000, without an order in council or any authority except simply the action of the department itself. And the country knew nothing about it until it came out in the course of the investigation of another department. Has the minister any report from the Falconer firm ?
Yes.
Would he have any objection to bringing it down?
I think it has been down for some time. Or, perhaps I am wrong about; it may be before the Public Accounts Committee.
But not before the House. Well, as we are called upon to pay the bill, the least we can expect is to have the report. What in brief, were the changes made by this firm in the system of bookkeeping?

I am not sufficiently expert to give the House a technical explanation. As a matter of fact, I do not know. And no person, unless he were an expert bookkeeper, would know even if he were told. I am assured by the management that the results are very satisfactory. I will be ready to bring down the report. It is a long report and it will take some time to copy. Maybe the copy before the Public Accounts Committee will be available.

Does not the minister think his statement rather odd? It may be his misfortune, but it certainly is not our fault that, when asked what has resulted from an expenditure of $50,000 he is compelled to say:	I cannot tell you and I do
not know that you would understand if I did tell you.
Well, it is true, isn't it ?

You must give the questioner the benefit of the doubt. Certainly, the question is perfectly germane to the subject. We can hardly allow $9,000 000 to go into the hands of the minister to be spent for something that he does not know and cannot tell. I think the minister ought to be able, in consultation with his deputy, to give the main points of the beneficial change

if there was a change, in the system of bookkeeping, in the first place, was the former system of bookkeeping on the Intercolonial a double-entry system?

Perhaps the hon. gentleman will find fault with me for not answering his question directly-but I am informed that the weakness of the old system was that we had not the detailed results that are required in modern railway work.
In what respect?

As to the cost of the service-cost per mile, and so on. Modern railways must keep these in great'detail, in order to report to the commission and governments and to apportion costs. While our system of bookkeeping may have given honest results so far as the country is concerned, it did not give us the exact results necessary in the management of our business and so we had to have the system modernised. I admit that I am not competent to discuss the details. But if I were buying a new style of locomotives-I submit this case to my hon. friend-I would decide on the basis of the reports of my engineers and other officials whom I have there for that purpose. And if it were demonstrated to me, that the engine could go at greater speed, or draw heavier trains I think that would be sufficient for me as head of the department, even though 1 could not explain the details of the working of that engine. So, in this case, I am not competent to go into detail of this accounting system. But the result of it is that our system is greatly improved. On the sheet that I now have before me, there are ninety items specified, giving expenses on a basis of monthly comparison. Under the old system we had only four or five heads altogether. For instance, with the old system, I could not have given the comparisons I gave this afternoon.

Well, the minister was not very full in his explanations this afternoon. If he gave us information which he would not have been able to give under the old system I do not know what he could have told us had he not had this new system. I should think he would have been confined simply to nodding his head. Could he not, with that sheet before him give the committee an idea of the difference between the information before and that which is given now? That would illustrate the change of system, I. should think.

This sheet shows the disbursements for the month under different headings. Under the old system we had four headings, not divided into subdivisions as in this statement. Under this system we have some ninety headings for March, 1908, March, 1907, the nine months ending at a certain date, and the twelve months ending a certain date. Then we have a sum-324i
mary at the end, showing at the end of every month, in each department, the expenses as compared with the corresponding month of the previous year.

That is a good illustration of what seems to have been done by that firm. For instance, instead of having these expenses divided into three or four large heads, you now run them down into the details. So you not only have a comparison between the whole expenditure, but you run that down into every branch, and find the comparative cost for each one. It is a differentiation of the whole system into a large number of details. But what I wanted to know was if that was done by other railway systems. There was not so much difficulty in adopting it here as to make it necessary to get a firm and pay them 9550,000 to help you introduce it. It seems to me that all that would have been necessary was to get the system of this differentiation from one of the great railroads that had adopted it, and get a practical man who had worked it out upon that railway, to indoctrinate your own men with it.

The most difficult thing is what the hon. gentleman calls the indoctrination. Men are wedded to an old system, and they often think it is better than a new system that you ask them to adopt. We had to work the system in gradually. The department had practically to keep a number of these men until they did the actual work of installing this new system, and doing it right beside our own men and teaching them as the work went along. In addition to that, we had to send them to different stations. These men were kept for quite a time doing the work with our men.

I am not disposed to say that the change in the system has not been a good one. But it seems to me it has been effected at a very large expense. Whether it was necessary to spend $50,000 for that teaching is a matter that puzzled me. It seems to me that you could have got three or four experts from a railway that had adopted this system, and these could have taught your own men. Is the system working satisfactorily ?
It is giving entire satisfaction.
Is there any clash between the Auditor General's Department and the system that was introduced by these gentlemen ?
There is no clash with the Auditor General's Department.

The audit system has been adopted by most of the large railways of

late years, both in Canada and the States. They have one man reporting upon their system of bookkeeping. I have seen two or three reports of railways about the size of the Intercolonial, and it would not require very much change to adapt the system to the Intercolonial. One of the most valuable features of the report of the auditors is the very strict line that is drawn between what shall be charged to capital account and what shall be charged to expenditure.
I think the report deals with that very matter.

If these experts have outlined carefully the different kinds of expenditures, what should go to capital and what should go to revenue, has the department that feature of the report and are you carrying it out ?

We have the report, and I may say that we are approximating to the principle laid down in that report. As I explained this afternoon we expect, by the new method we have adopted, to shortly be in a position to absolutely follow the lines of the report.	*
Then the minister is being indoctrinated?
Perhaps indoctrinated with the theory, but the practice is rapidly approximating to the point of indoctrination.
The minister will have to get a hustle on because some of the sentiments he gave expression to to-night do not appear to be in strict line with these principles.
Will the general report as to the system of bookkeeping and capital account be issued and distributed? I think it would be very useful if it were distributed to members.
We have it printed in the instruction book which contains what my hon. friend suggests as to the capital account, revenue and expenditure. I will be glad to send it to my hon. friend.
Will the minister bring down the report?
It will take some time to copy.
There is one in the Public Accounts Committee.
In that case I will bring it down.

Coming down to the item proposed, I would like to ask the minister if he w'ould be kind enough to give us the distribution of the $9,000,000. He has spent $50,000 in getting the indoctrination Mr. OSLER.
which brings out in detail what is absolutely necessary in order to come at a proper understanding of the working of the department. Now let us apply this doctrine of differentiation to the $9,000,000. The minister is asking for $9,000,000 and I would like him to divide this into the chief items and give the committee some little guide as to the points within which they should keep for each.

That has never been done in the history of the railway. I do not think it has ever been done in the history of any railway. The vote has never been asked in that way. I have not the figures divided in that way and they could not possibly be so divided.

Does the minister mean to say that he has had no estimate put before him of the amount that is to be devoted to advertising, salaries and wages and the different amounts that are to make up the large lines of expenditure? Surely no estimate can be made up to give $9,000,000 unless it is just simply to say:	We
will ask for what we asked for last year. Surely no estimate is made up unless it is made up in detail and by getting the bulk sum by adding the detailed estimates. The deputy minister must have the detailed estimates.

If my hon. friend will turn to pages S2, 83, 84 of the report of the Department of Railways and Canals he will find a detailed statement as to where these amounts went.
Maintenance of way and structures, $1,111,888.68.
Maintenance of equipment, $1,180,521.16.
The different heads of expenditure are given there. As a matter of fact, we can only take these items, and I imagine that the only way we can make an estimate upon these is to assume that the equipment will be increased as our business is increased. The only way we can do is to base the business of this year on last year's business, believing and hoping that the amount of business will be up to last year's at least. Last year we spent $9,000,000. We asked for an estimate of something like $7,000,000 and in the Supply estimates we had to ask for $1,400,000 more. Our estimate for next year is absolutely based upon the expenditure of last year.

Then the minister bears out what I have said, that in making up the estimates for the year he sat down and looked at the report of last year and found it totalled up so much. He came to the conclusion he would want as much this year and put it down. Does the minister mean to say that his officers do not provide him with an estimate, for instance, of the maintenance of way, or liow much will be spent for advertising, how much for ties

and other things of that kind, which are matters of absolute calculation? I do not ask for the details of everything. It would be impossible to get down to absolute truth in reference to all the details, but I cannot think that it is not possible to make a definite division of an estimate of the moneys voted by parliament.

This is one of the difficulties:	We have to ask on capital account,
more money than we spend every year because we have to provide enough for a certain work. Perhaps we have too much for a certain work. If you divide this up under special headings and tie us to these votes we cannot run the railway. You cannot run the railway in that particular way. We would have to ask for a larger vote than $9,000,000. We give a plain statement of what was done with the money last year, and we propose to do the same this year. If we had to specialize this it would make it impossible for a minister to accept the vote and run the road unless he asked for more money than he needed.

It means that you do not sit down and carefully calculate what you require for the road, thus setting yourself a limit, and endeavouring to work your road economically so as to keep within your appropriation, if it is possible to do so. The minister may ask a little more than he will probably expend but he decides as nearly as possible what he may require and he may add to it so as to be sure that he does not crimp himself.

My hon. friend must see the impracticability of applying his logic to the operation of a railway. This railway is hampered as no other railway is in having to come to parliament for supplies. If we had so much for maintenance of way for instance, and some unforeseen occurrence arose we could only use the money voted for maintenance of way and could not take from any other vote. We would therefore be in an awkward position. The only practical way is to hold the management responsible for the way in which the money is expended and allow the lump sum voted to be distributed as the interests of the road for the year may demand. There has got to be elasticity and flexibility in a vote for the operation of a railway or else you simply cannot carry it on.

There may be something in what the minister says, but so far as his argument goes about requiring money because of an accident or some unforeseen occurrence the minister has always power to get money, and his argument on that ground falls. Does not the minister think that it puts a check on extravagance and tends to good and economic administration that you should have your vote divided into different sections rather than to have it in a
lump sum. Of course it is very convenient to take a lump vote and apply it just as you please but the other system is in my opinion the better one. Suppose you take a vote for maintenance of way now and it is found to be insufficient, you can get a supplementary vote when parliament meets next November. Parliament is practically always within reach to give a supplementary vote if it be necessary.

I am firmly convinced that if my hon. friend thinks it out he will find it would be unworkable to divide this vote into details so much for each branch. While it sounds all right theoretically it would be impracticable in the working out.
I know my hon. friend does not want to hamper the railway.
No, but I would like to hamper the minister a little in some of his extravagant expenditures.
This minister does not need hampering as much as some hon. gentlemen opposite required to be hampered during their administration.
I am not so sure of that.

It is not reasonable to vote money for the working of a railway in detail unless you vote several millions of dollars more than you would vote under the present system, and if you did that it would be an incentive to extravagance rather than to economy in every department. We make as full a statement of our expenditure as any railroad company in the world ; there is no railway in the world so criticised by its stockholders as is the management of the Intercolonial Railway in this House ; there is no concealment, and with all that before the country it is unnecessary and impracticable to divide this vote up into sections.	[DOT]
Does not the minister have his officers prepare a general statement on which he bases his total estimate for the coming year ?
In making up the estimates they go into the different branches and take into consideration the expenditure of the previous year and the probable increased business of the coming year.
Are there no special changes ?

There are no special changes to come out of revenue. It is practically the same as last year. It may vary one way or the other. It cost $9,000,000 practically last year and will not cost much more next year.
Are you cutting the wages 1
We have not cut the wages at all; in fact all the men are asking for more.
Are you cutting any men out?

Some members, as the bon. member for Colchester tbis afternoon, complains that several men had been what we call set back for a time in order to relieve the condition. That is they are doing other work.
Are they not doing that on all railways in the country?
All roads are reducing expenditure. It is more difficult for a government road to reduce expenditure than an ordinary road, although we hope to keep the expenditure low.

What is the policy of the -department in this respect, to discharge some men and keep others employed full time or to keep all the men employed' on reduced time so as to keep their families in more or less comfort and when conditions improve and there is demand for more men, have the complete staff available? It has come to be recognized that in order to produce stability in service, as well as for the benefit of the homes of these people, it is better to keep the whole staff employed hut to run them on shorter hours.

The unions all over America govern that, the various brotherhoods of railway workers. As far as I recollect their rules are that a certain standard of salary must be maintained, that the men must earn a certain amount. I think under the rules we would have to drop the men rather than take the position suggested by my hon. friend, although in many cases I believe it to be preferable.

I do not think in any case the minister should be run by the union. The employment of these men should be made as regular as possible even if they only get one trip or one job where formerly they would have two or three. I do not think that the other method is -the proper way to treat the labouring men in this country. There should be some system, and I do not think any road could establish it better than the government road.

As I understood the bridges were built according to plans ap-Mr. GRAHAM.
proved by the city engineer of St. John and by the engineers of the Intercolonial Railway.

At page W-123, it appears the Montreal Cotton Company have received some $25,500 for cotton waste. I notice that the prices range from 6J cents to about 60 cents a pound. Was this by public tender or by private tender?
If my hon. friend will explain what he means by private tender?
As I understand your private tender it can be nothing more than a letter to those on the patronage list.
These are by tender, by circular I think. I give my friend the benefit of the doubt and say it is by circular.
This is a large item for material that is available in many parts of the country, and I would ask bow many of those circulars were sent out.

The minister will certainly have to get Falconer and his firm on again when the minister is asking $9,000,000 which he will not divide or give any particulars of. Then when the hon. gentleman is asked what was expended last year and how, he does not seem disposed to give the information.
What information ?
This very thing we have been talking of.

My hon. friend is mistaken about that as about the other. I tell him there was competition. If I had to give all the information he wants, it would necessitate my bringing over the particulars of every tender for the last year. I can get that Information if necessary, but it is impracticable to carry a list of the names of all the tenders and pile them up in the House. If he is anxious, I will get the list and let him have it in the morning.
Where is this Cotton Company situated ?
In Montreal.

Practically all the supplies, the minister purchased by the month. If the minister is compelled to purchase $2,000 worth of this material and $150,000 worth of iron and steel, there is no excuse for his not advertising throughout the country and getting the benefit of competition. If, on the other hand, he is

purchasing by the month from these stores, he must expect to pay the highest prices.
There is an item here for car repairs by other railways $41,000. What check has the Intercolonial on that ?
These repairs are paid under the standard rules of the Master Car Builders Association. All railways pay the same tariff.

Who is the judge of the necessity for repairs ? Suppose one of your cars employed on some other road, possibly in the United States, has to be repaired, who is to be the judge of the repairs required ?
The representative of the Master Car Builders Association on that; railroad is the judge.
And the Intercolonial, in repairing the cars of other roads, acts on the same principle ?
Yes.
What is the proportion of idle cars on the Intercolonial as compared with last year ?
, Last year we were something over 2,500 cars short of the regular supply. This year we are very near to what ought to be our normal supply.
The difference is measured* by the difference between your shortage last year and your having the normal number at present ?
Yes.
Does the minister see any improvement on what seemed to be a great abuse as to the number of Intercolonial cars that were outside the jurisdiction of the Intercolonial and in use on other roads?

That is remedied this year from the fact that the other roads do not want our cars and are glad to get rid of them and not have to pay the expense. Another idea we have been adopting is netting our pulp wood cars made in such a way that the roads on the other side of the line will not be able to use them for other traffic.
When they do use them, they pay a certain rate per day ?
All we get now is 25 cents a day. It used to be 50 cents.
Does that pay for the wear and tear ? There is a chance for great imposition by the bigger roads on the smaller in that respect.
Yes.
Have they not some regulations in the United States lately, compelling these railways to pay for the detention of cars ?

The roads are all members of the same association and the fee is the same. A couple of roads refused to remain in the association if the fees were not reduced and it was reduced to 25 cents. They were probably the chief offenders.
When your cars get over to the United States, do they keep them long before they send them back, if they want them ?

That often happens. We send an ordinary box car with pulp wood, and if the other road is short of rolling stock, they will send it on from one road to another and each railroad will keep it awhile. We will find a car sometimes out at the Rockies months before getting it back. We charge for the amount of time it is used, and the charge hardly pays for the wear and tear.
Who keeps the account ?
We have a regular car account.
BORDEN'. How do you know how long one road keeps it and then how long another road keeps it ?
Each road is supposed to report every day. We get information from the various lines where our car Is.
While they have that car and are running it around from road to road and repairing it when necessary, do they charge you for repairs ? If so how do you make up this item of $41,000 for car repairs ?
There are certain divisions as to repairs on different roads. They are under the rules of the Master Oar Builders' Association. We are all under the same rules and regulations.
But the minister does not know whether these are all charged up to the Intercolonial.
No, I can give that information .to-morrow.
It is something in the nature of a clearing house between banks.
It is and it isn't.

Is it all reported to some central accountant amongst the different roads, or do you have to enter this up as between yourselves and fifteen or twenty different roads in the United States ?

Mr, GRAHAM. The Master Car Builders' Association lay down rules as to what constitute repairs and what must be done. If there is a dispute in carrying that out, they adjudicate and give a decision.
Suppose a car is broken on a foreign road. Say, for instance, an Intercolonial car is running over the Boston and Maine and is smashed, the Intercolonial does not pay for that?

No, under the regulations the road that smashes the car pays.
Mr. ,T. D. REID. Why cannot the minister run the trains on time? A short time ago the minister gave me a statement of the running of the Maritime Express for several months, and I think he will agree that there were only about two days a month for three or four months when the train was on time. It was late by from five minutes to nine hours.

It is a large railway problem why trains do not run on time. In the first place, this is a long run-a thousand miles. We try to run on time, but I regret that we do not always succeed. If the hon. gentdeman will look carefully into it, I think he will see that, . in quite a number of instances, the lateness of the train is insignificapt-a matter of a few minutes. Of course, a matter of even five or ten minutes is sometimes enough to lose a connection. I remember that, in a matter of causing trains to connect which we discussed this session, we had to make quite an allowance for lateness. My own idea is that perhaps we make too many stops on this Maritime Express. We try, more than a company road would, to accommodate the smaller places. We have petitions from many of the smaller towns on the line, and I am quite unpopular in some of them because I do not have the train stop. There are many reasons why trains are late, but I think that, in this ease, one of the reasons is the many stops that we make.

I understand that this maritime express is supposed to be a fast train. It should run nearly on time. Take the Grand Trunk's International Limited-
I do not think it is late once in a month, but runs sharp on time always. Then take the train to the coast, which has a run of 3,000 miles, and it runs on time practically every day. Of course, a local train carrying express and required to stop often may easily be late. But I am told that one reason why this Maritime Express is late is that there are generally one or two government private cars on.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh.
What I am saying is that the International Limited, for instance, will not take on a private car. If this is

not the reason why the Maritime Express is late, theii I would like to know what the reason is. Out of thirty times in a month, I am sure it was late twenty-five times- I think that would be the average. If the Intercolonial is running a fast train it ought to run it on time, as the other roads do and not have it from ten minutes to nine hours late.
The hon. gentleman should know that he is wrong about the Canadian Pacific Railway fast train being on time. It was about nine hours late yesterday, I believe.
The limited train?

I think so. I am not saying that disparagingly for these difficulties will arise. We have the Ocean Limited which would correspond to the fast train on the Grand Trunk. No official cars are allowed to be carried on that train. But the Maritime Express is a through train and stops at as many places as possible to accommodate the people. It is not as fast a train as the Ocean Limited. I am confident that the lateness-which is liable to happen to any train-is not caused by official cars being carried.

Some time ago I asked about an accident that occurred on the Intercolonial between Montreal and Quebec. The train was off the track twice before it reached its destination. Are such accidents frequent?

If the hon. gentleman will look up the record, I think he will find that accidents are not more frequent than on any other road-perhaps they are less than on the majority of roads. I have been on the Grand Trunk road myself and it ran off three times between Toronto and Brock ville.
AVhat I want to know is, is the Intercolonial track in good condition?
Yes.
We have been here now since eleven o'clock, so far as this item is concerned, we have had a pretty good discussion on it. I think we might pass this item and retire to our virtuous couches.
Carried.
My hon. friend could not open his heart sufficiently to include the next item?
I think that ought to be discussed. I think the minister should be satisfied when he has $9,000,000 voted.

I am not complaining. But there will be many items of capital expenditure for the canals-and this is a canal
.TTTXE 10, 1908
item-on which we can have as full a discussion as lion, gentlemen may wish.
The trouble is that, when it is put off, we never have a chance to discuss the matter. I do not think it is fair to ask to have the item slide through without discussion.
This item includes the men on the canals, and, if a Supply Bill is put through, it would be well to have the money to pay the men.
What is the amount?

It is $1,016,408 including the amount for staff and repairs. I am not urging it, but I am simply pointing out there are many items of capital expenditure on which I will guarantee that full opportunity should be given for discussion.
It does not seem like having a meal when you take it off the table.

I am simply pointing out the reason why I would like to have this amount voted.
